The Health Emergency Response Data System, through which LHCSAs report weekly, including patient census by licensed county.

procedures: The Administrator will make sure an HCS account is requested and activated for each agency operated, and will have the HCS Coordinator keep the activation records.
The Administrator will appoint an HCS Coordinator and at least one trained backup. The backup must be able to open the account and respond to requests whenever the Coordinator is out.

The HCS Coordinator will assign HCS roles to named individuals. The roles are Administrator; Director of Patient Services; Emergency Response Coordinator; HCS Coordinator; Criminal History Record Check (CHRC) Authorized Person; Home Care Registry Agency Updater; and Home Care Registry Agency Viewer. The Coordinator will record each assignment on the HCS Role Assignment Log with name, role, start date and the Administrator's approval.

The Administrator will designate at least two individuals as Home Care Registry designees under 10 NYCRR 403.3(a). Only these designees may submit data to the registry (403.3(c)). The registry procedure is in PER-03.

The HCS Coordinator or backup will log in to HCS on every business day, review all new alerts, messages, surveys and requests, and record the check on the HCS Daily Access Log (date, time, initials, items found).

If neither the Coordinator nor the backup can log in on a given business day, the Administrator will personally ensure the check is done. The Administrator will not leave the account unchecked for a full business day.

The agency will keep HCS coverage throughout its posted hours of operation. The Coordinator will post a coverage schedule showing who is responsible each day, and the backup will cover planned absences.

The HCS Coordinator will forward each DOH request or alert to the responsible person (Administrator, Director of Patient Services or Emergency Response Coordinator) the same business day, and will log the date received, the person assigned and the due date.

The agency will acknowledge each DOH request the same business day it is found and will respond within the deadline stated in the request. If the request states no deadline, the agency will respond within two business days. The Administrator will review the log weekly for overdue items.

The HCS Coordinator will complete the weekly HERDS report, which includes patient census by licensed county. The reporting window opens Tuesday at 8:00 a.m. and closes Thursday at 2:00 p.m. The Coordinator will submit by Wednesday close of business, and the backup will cover if the Coordinator is out. Questions go to hcstatrpts@health.ny.gov.

The HCS Coordinator will review the communication directory at least monthly, using the Monthly Directory Review Checklist. The review confirms the 24/7 facility contact (name, title, phone) and the Office of the Administrator information (Administrator name, address, phone, email) are correct, and corrects any entry that is wrong.

The agency will update the directory within one business day of any change in the Administrator, Director of Patient Services, Emergency Response Coordinator, 24/7 contact, address or phone number, without waiting for the monthly review.

The 24/7 facility contact will be staffed through an on-call schedule maintained by the Director of Patient Services. The on-call person must answer calls promptly and know how to reach the Administrator.
When a role-holder leaves or changes jobs, the HCS Coordinator will remove or reassign that person's HCS and registry access within one business day and will record it on the HCS Role Assignment Log.
The Administrator will review and sign this HCS coverage policy at least annually, and whenever the roles, hours or account structure change. The review date will be recorded on the policy.
The Administrator will report HCS compliance (daily-access completion, response times, directory review dates) to the QI Committee at least annually (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and makes sure the agency has an HCS account, adequate staff and a current emergency contact arrangement (10 NYCRR 766.9).
Appoints the Coordinator and backup, approves role assignments, ensures daily access and timely response, signs the annual review.
Manages the account, logs in daily, routes requests, submits HERDS, updates the directory at least monthly and keeps logs.
Provides coverage during absences and holds the knowledge needed to maintain the account.
Responds to clinical and patient-care requests from DOH and maintains the on-call schedule for the 24/7 contact.
Receives and acts on emergency alerts and ensures the emergency contacts in the directory work (see SAF-05 and SAF-06).
Performs CHRC functions assigned in HCS (see PER-04).

responsibilities.role: Home Care Registry Updater and Viewer designees
responsibilities.duty: Enter and view registry data under Part 403. At least two are designated, and only they may submit data.

documentation: HCS account activation records for each agency operated
HCS Role Assignment Log (names, roles, dates, approval)
HCS Daily Access Log
DOH Request Tracking Log (date received, assignee, due date, date answered)
Weekly HERDS submission confirmations
Monthly Directory Review Checklists
On-call schedule for the 24/7 facility contact
Annual policy review signature page
Home Care Registry designee designation records

policies.title: Change of Ownership, Transfer of Interests and Management Changes
policies.applies_to: Governing authority, owners, officers, directors, members, shareholders, Administrator and anyone negotiating a transfer of interest or a management arrangement for [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure no change in ownership, control or management of [AGENCY NAME] takes effect without the notice to DOH and the approvals that New York law requires, so the agency never operates outside the terms of its license.
policies.policy:
A license issued under Public Health Law Article 36 belongs to the approved operator and is not transferable. [AGENCY NAME] will not transfer, sell, assign or give up any ownership interest or control, and will not enter any management contract, until DOH has been notified, an application has been submitted through NYSE-CON, and the approval required by law has been received. Any change requires review for character, competence, financial feasibility and public need under Public Health Law §3605 and 10 NYCRR §765-1.2 and §765-1.16. The agency will give accurate, complete disclosure at all times, because failing to disclose a change can void an approval. This policy meets the following items on the Applicant Worksheet (p.13), Change of Ownership policy/procedure:
- WS-COO.1: what constitutes a change of ownership, transfer of interests, stock or acquisition (see Definitions and procedures 1-3).
- WS-COO.2: notification to the Department (procedures 4-6).
- WS-COO.3: submission of an application to the Department (procedures 7-9).
- WS-COO.4: approval by the Public Health and Health Planning Council, before the change takes effect (procedures 10-12).

definitions.definition: Any transfer, sale or assignment of the agency, its operations or its license to another person or entity, including the transfer of stock, membership interests, partnership interests or other ownership interests, or the acquisition of control of the agency, whether in one transaction or a series.
Any change in who holds an ownership or membership interest in the agency's operator, including adding, removing or changing owners, stockholders or members, or a change in their percentages.
Gaining the power to direct the agency's management or policies, whether through ownership, voting rights, contract or another arrangement.
An agreement under which another party manages or operates all or part of the agency. It requires prior written consent of the Commissioner of Health under 10 NYCRR 766.9(m).
The Public Health and Health Planning Council, which approves, contingently approves or disapproves LHCSA applications.
The DOH electronic Certificate of Need system used to file LHCSA establishment and change-of-ownership applications.

procedures: Before any discussion that could lead to a sale, transfer, merger or new investor, the owner or officer involved will inform the Administrator and the governing authority in writing.

The Administrator and the governing authority will decide whether the proposed transaction is a change of ownership, a transfer of interests or an acquisition of control, using the definitions in this policy. If there is any doubt, they will treat it as a change that requires DOH review and ask DOH.

The Administrator will tell every party to the transaction in writing that the license cannot be transferred and that the change cannot take effect until DOH and PHHPC approvals are in place. No party may take control of the agency, its records or its patients before then.

The Administrator will notify DOH of the proposed change before it takes place. The Administrator will contact the Bureau of Home Care Licensure and Certification at homecareliccert@health.ny.gov for pre-filing questions and will confirm the filing steps in writing.
The Administrator will keep a copy of the notice and DOH's reply in the Ownership Change File.

If the proposed change involves a management contract, the Administrator will submit the proposal to DOH at least 60 days before its proposed effective date, as 10 NYCRR 766.9(m) requires, and will not sign or begin it until the Commissioner has given written consent. Franchise agreements are handled the same way under 10 NYCRR 766.9(n).

The governing authority will authorize the application by resolution. The Administrator will gather the information DOH requires about each new or continuing owner, officer and director, including identifying information, background and character and competence information, and financial information.

The agency will show financial feasibility through working capital of at least two months of estimated operating expenses, documented as 10 NYCRR 765-1.2 requires and confirmed by a certified public accountant.

The Administrator will file the application electronically through NYSE-CON and send the application fee in the amount DOH requires (the fee under Public Health Law §3605 is $2,000 for LHCSA applications, and the check is due within 30 days of NYSE-CON submission). The agency will answer DOH questions about the application promptly, in writing, and through its HCS account.

The agency will not leave out or misstate any fact in the application. If any application information changes while the application is pending, the Administrator will update DOH in writing right away.

The application is reviewed by DOH and submitted to PHHPC. PHHPC considers public need, character and competence, and financial resources. The Administrator will track the PHHPC meeting schedule and the status of the application, and will report to the governing authority after each step.

The change will take effect only after PHHPC approval and any conditions DOH attaches have been met. The Administrator will confirm approval in writing and the effective date. Until then, the current operator remains fully responsible for the agency, the patients and compliance.

After approval, the Administrator will update the HCS directory (GOV-07), the P&P manual (GOV-03), the agency brochure and public information (GOV-02), contracts (GOV-06), insurance, payer enrollments and MLTC contracts, and will tell patients and staff in writing of any change that affects them.

The Administrator will make sure patient records and personnel records stay secure and available throughout the transition, and that ownership of the records is addressed in the transaction documents (see REC-02).
At each annual governing authority meeting, the Administrator will have each owner and officer confirm in writing that no unreported transfer of interests or change of control has taken place.

responsibilities.duty: Approves any proposed change, authorizes the application, and ensures no change takes effect before required DOH and PHHPC approval.
Disclose any proposed transfer or change of control to the Administrator and governing authority before it occurs, and provide complete and accurate information.
Notifies DOH, prepares and files the NYSE-CON application, tracks approval, updates agency documents and keeps the Ownership Change File.
Makes sure patient care and RN supervision continue without interruption during any transition.
Advise on transaction structure and certify working capital and financial information.

documentation: Ownership Change File (notices to DOH, replies, application, approval letters)
Governing authority resolutions authorizing an application
NYSE-CON filing confirmation and fee payment record
PHHPC approval and any conditions
Management contract and Commissioner consent letter
Annual owner/officer attestations of no unreported change
Records of notices to patients, staff and payers

policies.title: Amendment of the License (Counties, Services, Sites)
policies.applies_to: Governing authority, Administrator, Director of Patient Services and any staff involved in planning expansion or relocation
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] provides services only in the counties, for the services and from the sites that are on its license, and obtains DOH approval before any of them changes.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] will not add a county, add a service, or change or add a site or office location until DOH has approved the change. We will provide care only within the licensed service area and the licensed services (Public Health Law §3605). New counties remain subject to the public need review under 10 NYCRR §765-1.16. After any approved amendment the agency will update its P&P manual, HCS directory and brochure. This policy meets the following items on the Applicant Worksheet (p.13), Amendment of the License policy/procedure:
- WS-AMD.1: what constitutes an amendment (adding a county, adding a service, changing or adding a site or office location; see Definitions).
- WS-AMD.2: notification to and approval by the Department before acting (procedures 3-5 and 9).
- WS-AMD.3: submitting required materials to the Department as applicable to the type of amendment (procedures 6-8).

definitions.definition: A change to the terms of the agency's license that requires DOH approval, including adding a county to the service area, adding a service (nursing, home health aide, personal care), and changing or adding a site or office location.
The counties listed on the agency's license. An initial license covers up to five counties in one DOH region, with one contiguous county in another region allowed.
The DOH regional office that reviews the P&P manual and conducts surveys for the agency.
The review in 10 NYCRR 765-1.16, under which there is a rebuttable presumption of no need in a county where 5 or more LHCSAs each actively serve 25 or more patients.

procedures: The Administrator will review the license each quarter and before any expansion planning, to confirm the authorized counties, services and sites, and will record the review in the License Review Log.

Staff must not accept a patient, assign a visit or advertise a service outside the licensed counties or services. The intake staff will check each patient's county of residence against the license before acceptance (see SVC-02).

When the governing authority or Administrator proposes to add a county, add a service, or change or add a site or office location, the Administrator will write a short proposal that states the change, the reason, the proposed date and the effect on patients and staff.
The governing authority will review the proposal and authorize it by resolution before the agency applies. The resolution will be placed in the Amendment File.

The Administrator will notify DOH of the proposal before taking any action and will ask the regional home care office or homecareapplications@health.ny.gov which materials are needed for the type of amendment. The agency will not begin services in a new county, begin a new service, or move or open an office until DOH has approved it in writing.

For a new county, the Administrator will prepare the application materials DOH requires, including evidence of public need under 10 NYCRR 765-1.16 and, where required, the commitment to serve hard-to-reach groups, and will check the current public-need status of the county.

For a new service, the Administrator will prepare the materials DOH requires for the service, including the staffing plan, qualifications, policies and the RN supervision arrangements. For example, adding nursing services requires licensed RN staff and nursing policies.

For a new or changed site or office location, the Administrator will prepare the materials DOH requires, which may include the address, lease, floor plan, record storage arrangements, access to patient records and prompt telephone contact (10 NYCRR 766.9(f)).

The Administrator will submit the complete application and materials to DOH as directed, answer questions promptly, and keep proof of submission. If DOH needs more information, the Administrator will provide it by the date DOH sets.

The Administrator will track the application and report its status to the governing authority. The agency will act on an amendment only after receiving DOH's written approval and any conditions, and will record the effective date.

Within 30 days after the effective date, the Administrator will update the P&P manual (GOV-03), the HCS communication directory (GOV-07), the agency brochure and public information (GOV-02), the emergency plan and patient roster (SAF-05), contracts and insurance, and payer and MLTC records.

The Administrator will train staff on the change before the first visit or day of operation that depends on it, including new scheduling areas, new service duties and the new address, and will record the training.
The Administrator will report the status of every amendment to the QI Committee at least annually (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Authorizes each proposed amendment and ensures no change is made before DOH approval.
Reviews the license regularly, prepares and files amendment materials, communicates with DOH, and updates agency documents after approval.
Confirms RN supervision, staffing and clinical policies are in place for any new county or service.
Accept and schedule only patients and services within the licensed counties and scope.
Updates the HCS directory after each approved amendment.

documentation: License and License Review Log
Amendment File (proposal, governing authority resolution, DOH correspondence, application materials, approval)
Proof of submission to DOH
Updated P&P manual, directory and brochure with revision dates
Staff training records for the change

policies.title: Patient Rights and Responsibilities (Notice, Documentation and Exercise of Rights)
policies.applies_to: All patients, their legally authorized representatives, and all agency staff, including intake staff, RNs, aides and supervisors
policies.purpose: To make sure every patient of [AGENCY NAME] receives, understands and can exercise the rights guaranteed by 10 NYCRR 766.1, and that we can show it in the clinical record.
policies.policy:
The governing authority adopts this policy as the agency's written patient-rights policy and procedure under 10 NYCRR 766.1(a). Every patient (or the patient's legally authorized representative) will receive the rights in writing and have them explained verbally before care starts, and receipt will be documented in the clinical record (766.1(a)(1); 766.6(a)(9)). All care staff will know and follow these rights (766.1(b)). This policy meets the following items on the Applicant Worksheet (pp.1 and 5) and 10 NYCRR 766.1(a):
- WS-PR.1 (written and verbal notification of patient's rights) and WS-ADM.6 (written notification of patient rights): procedures 1-4.
- WS-PR.2 (documentation of providing patient rights): procedure 5.
- WS-PR.3 (the services the agency provides) and WS-PR.7 (services, and when and how services are to be provided): procedure 6.
- WS-PR.8 (right to participate in planning their care): procedure 7.
- WS-PR.9 (name, title and functions of who will provide services): procedure 8.
- WS-PR.10 (any changes to their plan of care): procedure 9.
- WS-PR.11 (right to refuse care and treatment, including refusing advanced home health aide tasks): procedure 10.
- WS-PR.12 (right to voice complaints and grievances) and WS-PR.13 (right to contact the NYS Department of Health): procedure 11 and CR-03.
- WS-PR.14 (treated with consideration, respect and dignity): procedure 12.
- WS-PR.15 (privacy, including confidential treatment of patient records) and WS-PR.16 (right to refuse the release of records to any outside agency): procedure 13 and CR-04.
- WS-PR.17 (legal representative if the patient lacks capacity): procedure 14.
- 766.1(a): the full written rights notice, as set out in procedures 1-14.
The cost, charges and payer information required by 766.1(a)(2)-(3) is covered in CR-02.

definitions.definition: A person receiving nursing, home health aide or personal care services from the agency, including Medicaid and MLTC plan members and private-pay clients.
A person with legal authority to act for a patient who lacks capacity, such as a health care agent under a health care proxy, a court-appointed guardian, or another person authorized by law.
Tasks beyond the usual duties of a home health aide that a patient has the right to refuse (766.1(a)(12)).
Any retaliation for exercising a right or making a complaint, including reduced service, threats, a changed schedule or discharge.

procedures: The intake or admission staff member will give the Patient Rights and Responsibilities notice in writing to each patient or the legally authorized representative before the first visit and before care starts. The notice will be in plain language and in the patient's preferred language, or will be interpreted (see CR-06).

The RN or trained intake staff will explain each right verbally, check understanding, and answer questions. For a patient with a hearing, vision or cognitive impairment, staff will use an accommodation (large print, reading aloud, interpreter or the representative).

The written notice will include the rights listed in this policy, the agency name, address and telephone number, the name of the Administrator, how to make a complaint to the agency, and the NYS DOH home care complaint hotline: [DOH HOME CARE COMPLAINT HOTLINE NUMBER – confirm the current number with DOH before printing; historically 1-800-628-5972].
The notice will state the patient's right to complain to the NYS Department of Health, Office of Health Systems Management, and that complaints may be made without reprisal.

The patient or representative will sign and date an acknowledgment of receipt. If the person cannot or will not sign, the staff member will document the reason and the date, time and manner in which the notice was given. The original acknowledgment goes in the clinical record (766.6(a)(9)), and the patient keeps a copy of the notice.

Before care starts, the RN or intake staff will tell the patient what services the agency will provide and when and how they will be provided (frequency, days and approximate hours), consistent with the authorization, the plan of care and the service agreement.

The patient will be told of the right to take part in planning care. The RN will invite the patient and representative to take part in the assessment, plan of care and each update, will record their preferences and goals in the plan (see SVC-06), and will document their participation. Care planning will follow person-centered principles, including for patients in Medicaid home and community-based programs (42 CFR 441.301(c)).

Before care starts, and again whenever the assigned worker changes, the patient will be told the name, title and function of each person who will provide services (RN, aide, supervisor). Aides will wear identification and will give their name and title at the first visit.

The agency will tell the patient before any change in services or in the plan of care, and the RN will document the notice and the patient's response. If an authorization or a payer decision changes services, the Director of Patient Services will explain the change and refer the patient to the MLTC plan or district for appeal rights as appropriate.

The patient may refuse any care or treatment, and may refuse advanced home health aide tasks (766.1(a)(12)). A staff member who is told of a refusal will tell the RN. The RN will explain the possible consequences, document the refusal and the patient's understanding, notify the ordering practitioner and payer or plan as appropriate, and update the plan of care. Refusal will not by itself lead to discharge or any reprisal.

The patient may complain to the agency or to DOH at any time without reprisal. Any staff member who receives a complaint will follow CR-03. The agency prohibits retaliation, and any report of reprisal will be investigated by the Administrator.

All staff will treat patients with consideration, respect and dignity, will use the name the patient prefers, will respect cultural and personal choices, and will protect the patient's privacy during care. Disrespectful treatment is addressed under PER-10 and, when it may be abuse, SAF-01.

The patient's records are confidential. Staff will not release or discuss patient information except as the patient authorizes or the law allows (see CR-04 and REC-01). The patient may refuse to let the agency release records to any outside agency, except as the law requires or permits. The agency will give the HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices (45 CFR 164.520) no later than the first service delivery and will document the patient's acknowledgment, or the effort to get it.

If a patient lacks capacity, the legally authorized representative exercises the patient's rights (766.1(c)). Staff will ask for and copy the documents establishing authority (health care proxy, guardianship order or other) and file them in the record. The patient will still be told about the care and involved in decisions to the extent they are able.

Staff will be trained on this policy at orientation before providing care and at least annually (see PER-05) and will sign that they have been trained (766.1(b)). The Director of Patient Services will confirm the training.
The RN supervisor will check at each supervisory visit that the patient still has a copy of the rights notice and knows how to make a complaint, and will document this.
The QI Committee will audit a sample of records each quarter for a signed rights acknowledgment dated before the first visit and will report gaps to the governing authority (see GOV-04).
The Administrator will review this policy at least annually and update the rights notice whenever the law, the hotline number or the agency's contact information changes.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts and amends the patient-rights policy and ensures it is carried out (766.9(d)).
Ensures the rights notice is current, staff are trained, and reprisal is not tolerated.
Explains rights, involves patients in care planning, documents refusals and changes, and checks rights awareness during supervision.
Deliver the written notice, obtain the signed acknowledgment, and file it before care starts.
Know and follow patient rights, give their name and title, treat patients with respect, and report complaints and refusals.
Provides accurate information, takes part in planning, tells the agency of changes in condition or schedule, and treats staff with respect.

documentation: Signed Patient Rights acknowledgment in the clinical record (766.6(a)(9))
Copy of the rights notice used, with revision date
Documentation of verbal explanation and interpreter or accommodation used
Care plan participation notes and refusal-of-care documentation
Documents establishing a representative's authority
HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgment
Staff rights training records
QI audit results

policies.title: Service Agreement, Statement of Services, Charges and Payer Liability
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, billing staff, RNs, the Administrator, and all patients and representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure every patient is told, in writing and before care starts, which services will be provided, what they cost, what third-party payers are expected to pay and what the patient must pay, and is told within 30 calendar days of any change.
policies.policy:
Before care starts, [AGENCY NAME] will give each patient or representative a written statement of services and charges (10 NYCRR 766.1(a)(2)) and will tell the patient how much third-party payers (Medicaid, MLTC plans, insurers) are expected to pay and how much the patient must pay (766.1(a)(3)). Any change will be given to the patient orally and in writing within 30 calendar days of the date the agency learns of the change (766.1(a)(3)(i)-(ii)). The agency will also make its charges and accepted payment sources public (766.9(e)). The patient or representative signs the service agreement and informed consent. This policy meets the following items on the Applicant Worksheet (pp.1 and 5):
- WS-PR.4 (the cost of the services): procedures 2-3.
- WS-PR.5 (the patient's responsibility for payment after insurance/third-party payers): procedures 4-6.
- WS-PR.6 (any changes to services in 30 calendar days from the date of change): procedures 9-11.
- WS-ADM.5 (notification/explanation of costs, insurance and expectation of payment): procedures 1-8.

definitions.definition: The written document listing the services the agency will provide, the rate or charge for each, how charges are billed and when payment is due.
A payer other than the patient, such as Medicaid, a Medicaid Managed Long Term Care (MLTC) plan, Medicare, or private insurance.
The written agreement between the agency and the patient or representative describing services, schedule, charges, responsibilities and how either may end services.
Any amount the patient owes, such as private-pay charges, co-payments, deductibles, or the cost of services not covered or not authorized by the payer.

procedures: Intake staff will determine the patient's payer source(s) at referral and confirm authorization, coverage and eligibility with the payer, local district or MLTC plan before the first visit (see SVC-03 and SVC-17).

Before care starts, intake staff or the RN will give the patient or representative a written Statement of Services and Charges. It lists each service, the rate or charge, how it will be billed and when payment is due. The statement is dated and in plain language and in the patient's language or interpreted (see CR-06).

The statement will show the current agency charges for private-pay services [AGENCY PRIVATE-PAY RATE SCHEDULE], and for Medicaid or MLTC patients will state that the agency is paid under the plan or Medicaid rate.

Before care starts, the RN or intake staff will explain verbally and in writing how much each third-party payer is expected to pay, based on the authorization or coverage verified, and how much the patient must pay, including any co-payment, deductible, private-pay hours or non-covered services. If the patient owes nothing, the statement will say so.

The agency will not ask a Medicaid or MLTC patient to pay for authorized services, and will not bill the patient for amounts that the payer is required to cover, except where the law permits and the patient has been told in writing.

If the amount the patient must pay cannot be determined before care starts, the agency will tell the patient this, explain how and when it will be determined, and give the patient a good-faith estimate.

The patient or representative will sign and date the service agreement and informed consent after the statement of services and payer information have been explained (see SVC-02). The patient receives a copy. If the patient cannot sign, the reason and the witness are documented. The original goes in the clinical record.
The agency will keep its current charges and accepted payment sources available to the public on request and in its public information materials, as required by 766.9(e) (see GOV-02).

When the agency learns of a change in charges, payer coverage, authorization, hours or patient responsibility, the Administrator or billing supervisor will tell the patient or representative orally, and will follow with a written notice, as soon as possible and in all cases within 30 calendar days of the date the agency learned of the change (766.1(a)(3)(i)-(ii)).

The written notice of change will state what is changing, the effective date, the reason, the new amount the payer is expected to pay, the new amount the patient must pay, and whom to call with questions. For a change in Medicaid or MLTC authorization, the notice will also refer the patient to the plan or district for appeal rights.

The person giving the notice will document the date, time, method and the person told in the clinical record and on the Notice of Change Log. The patient or representative will be asked to acknowledge the notice.

If a change would reduce or end services, the RN will assess the patient's needs and follow SVC-14 and SVC-15 as applicable. The agency will not stop care without the notice and planning those policies require.

The billing supervisor will review each month's invoices against signed agreements and authorizations to confirm the patient was not charged more than agreed. Errors are corrected and the patient is refunded promptly.
Questions or complaints about charges will be handled under CR-03.
The QI Committee will audit a sample of records at least quarterly for a signed statement of services and charges, signed service agreement and documented notice of changes (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the agency's charges and ensures charges and payment sources are public (766.9(e)).
Ensures statements, agreements and notices of change are correct and timely and that billing follows this policy.
Verify payer, prepare and explain the statement of services and charges, and obtain signatures before care starts.
Explains services and payer expectations, and documents notices of change in the record.
Bills accurately, monitors changes in coverage or authorization, and sends written notices within 30 calendar days.
Reviews and signs the agreement and pays any amounts that are the patient's responsibility.

documentation: Signed Statement of Services and Charges
Signed service agreement and informed consent
Payer verification and authorization records
Notice of Change Log and copies of written notices
Documentation of oral notice (date, method, person told)
Current public charge schedule
Billing audit and refund records

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All patients, representatives and family members; all agency staff who may receive a complaint; the Administrator, the governing authority and the QI Committee
policies.purpose: To give patients a simple, safe and fair way to raise concerns about their care or the agency, to make sure every complaint is logged, investigated, answered and appealable, and to use complaints to improve quality.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] will maintain a written patient complaint and grievance procedure as required by 10 NYCRR 766.9(j). Every complaint, oral or written, will be recorded in a complaint log, investigated and resolved. The agency will give a written response to all written complaints, and to oral complaints if requested, within 15 days of the investigation findings. Complainants will be told of the right to appeal. A member or committee of the governing authority will review each appeal and notify the complainant within 30 days. Complainants will also be told of the right to complain to the NYS Department of Health. No patient or staff member will suffer reprisal for making a complaint (766.1(a)(7)-(9)). All complaints will go to the QI Committee. This policy meets the following items on the Applicant Worksheet (pp.1 and 8):
- WS-PR.18 (procedure to voice complaints and grievances): procedures 1-3.
- WS-PR.19 (NYS Department of Health complaint hotline number): procedure 4.
- WS-GA.12 (development and implementation of a patient complaint or grievance procedure): this entire policy.
- WS-GA.13 (maintain a record of complaints/concerns/grievances): procedure 5.
- WS-GA.14 (document receipt, investigation and resolution): procedures 5-8.
- WS-GA.15 (written response within 15 days of investigation findings): procedure 9.
- WS-GA.16 (advise the complainant of the right to appeal): procedure 10.
- WS-GA.17 (review the appeal and notify the complainant within 30 days of the appeal): procedures 11-12.
- WS-GA.18 (advised of the right to complain to the DOH): procedure 4.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction or concern, oral or written, made by or for a patient about care, staff, safety, billing, privacy, scheduling or any agency practice.
The record in which the agency documents each complaint's receipt, investigation, findings, response, appeal and resolution.
A request by the complainant that the governing authority review the agency's decision on the complaint.
Any retaliation against a person for complaining, including reduced or changed services, threats or discharge.

procedures: The agency will give every patient, at admission and with the patient rights notice, written information on how to make a complaint: by telephone to [PHONE], in writing to [ADDRESS], by email, in person, or through a representative. The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], is the complaint officer. Complaints may be made anonymously.

Any staff member who receives a complaint, orally or in writing, will treat it seriously, thank the complainant, and report it to the Director of Patient Services or Administrator by the end of the next business day. Staff will help patients with disabilities or limited English proficiency to make a complaint (see CR-06). Staff must never discourage a complaint.
If a complaint reports abuse, neglect, exploitation or an injury, the staff member will immediately follow SAF-01 and SAF-02 and make sure the patient is safe, in addition to this procedure.

The complaint notice, and the written response to each complainant, will say that the complainant may complain to the NYS Department of Health (Office of Health Systems Management) at any time, whether or not they use the agency's process. The notice will print the DOH home care complaint hotline: [DOH HOME CARE COMPLAINT HOTLINE NUMBER – confirm the current number with DOH before printing; historically 1-800-628-5972]. Complainants will be told their rights to complain to DOH, to appeal, and to be free of reprisal.

Within one business day of receipt, the Administrator or designee will enter the complaint in the Complaint Log: date and time received, name of complainant and patient, how received, nature of the complaint, person who received it and the assigned investigator.
The Administrator will acknowledge the complaint to the complainant, orally or in writing, within 2 business days, and will explain the steps and expected timing.

The Administrator or the Director of Patient Services will investigate promptly. The investigator will interview the complainant, the patient and relevant staff, review the clinical record, schedules and EVV data, and note findings in writing. The person complained about will not investigate the complaint. Clinical complaints are reviewed by the RN Director. Urgent safety issues are corrected immediately.

The investigator will decide whether the complaint is substantiated, will decide what corrective action is needed (retraining, discipline, schedule or process changes, a refund), and will record the findings, the corrective action and the date of completion in the log.

The Administrator will send a written response to every written complaint, and to every oral complaint if the complainant asks, within 15 days of the investigation findings. The response will describe the findings and action taken, in plain language and the complainant's language or interpreted.

The written response will advise the complainant of the right to appeal to the governing authority if not satisfied, how to appeal (in writing or orally to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] at [PHONE]), and of the right to complain to DOH.

When an appeal is received, the Administrator will log it the same business day and send it to the governing authority. A member or committee of the governing authority who was not involved in the original decision will review the complaint, the investigation file and any new information from the complainant.

The governing authority member or committee will decide the appeal and the agency will notify the complainant of the decision, in writing, within 30 days of receiving the appeal. The notice will again state the right to complain to DOH. The result is recorded in the log.

Where a complaint concerns an MLTC plan's or the local district's authorization of hours or services (for example, a decision under 18 NYCRR 505.14), the agency will still log and review the complaint, will explain that the plan or district decides authorization, and will help the patient contact the plan or district to use its own grievance, appeal or fair hearing process. The agency's own procedure does not replace those rights.

The agency will not retaliate against any patient or staff member who makes a complaint. The Administrator will check with the patient at 30 days to confirm that services have not been affected. Any staff member who retaliates is subject to discipline (see PER-10).

The Administrator will send a summary of all complaints and their outcomes to the QI Committee for review at each quarterly meeting. The Committee will review all complaint cases, look for trends, recommend corrective action and report in writing to the governing authority (see GOV-04).

The agency will keep complaint records, including the log, investigation files, responses and appeals, for 3 years after resolution, and in the patient's clinical record where they concern patient care (see REC-03).
The Administrator will review this policy each year, and whenever the DOH hotline number changes, and will update notices to patients.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this procedure; a member or committee reviews appeals and ensures a decision is sent within 30 days.
Serves as complaint officer, ensures logging, investigation, written responses within 15 days, and correct follow-up.
Investigates clinical complaints, supervises corrective action and checks on the patient after resolution.
Accept and report complaints within one business day, help patients complain, and never retaliate.
Reviews all complaints and trends at least quarterly and reports to the governing authority.

documentation: Complaint Log (receipt, investigation, resolution, response, appeal)
Investigation notes and corrective action records
Written responses to complainants and appeal decisions
Governing authority appeal review records
Complaint notice with DOH hotline given to patients
QI Committee minutes and complaint summaries
Complaint records retained for 3 years after resolution

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers, the governing authority and QI committee members of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of every patient and the confidentiality of patient records, to make sure records are released only as the patient authorizes or the law permits, and to meet HIPAA requirements for notice, safeguards, training and breach response.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] protects each patient's privacy and keeps every patient record confidential. This policy meets Applicant Worksheet p.1 item WS-PR.15 — the patient's right to privacy, including confidential treatment of his/her patient records (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(11)). It also meets Applicant Worksheet p.1 item WS-PR.16 — the patient's right to refuse the release of his/her records to any outside agency. Patient information is released to an outside party only with the patient's (or legally authorized representative's) written authorization, or where federal or New York law permits or requires release without authorization. Patients are told in writing, and orally on request, that they may refuse release. Refusing release never affects the patient's care or services. Records are kept secure and confidential, whether on paper or electronic, and electronic records can be printed on request (10 NYCRR §766.12(b)). Each patient record is confidential (10 NYCRR §766.6(a)). Written safeguards protect records against loss and unauthorized access and govern their use, removal and release (10 NYCRR §766.6(e)). Every patient receives the HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices. All staff are trained at hire and every year. Breaches are reported and handled under HIPAA, 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164. Patient privacy and record confidentiality are included in the patient rights information given before care starts (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(1)).

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health information about a patient in any form (paper, electronic or spoken), including name, address, diagnosis, services, schedule and payment information.

A signed, dated written permission from the patient or legally authorized representative allowing release of named information to a named person or organization for a stated purpose, with an expiration date and a statement of the right to revoke.
The HIPAA notice describing how the agency uses and discloses PHI and the patient's privacy rights.

An acquisition, access, use or disclosure of PHI not permitted by HIPAA that compromises the security or privacy of the PHI, unless a documented risk assessment shows a low probability that the PHI was compromised.
A person with legal authority to act for a patient who lacks capacity, who exercises the patient's rights under 10 NYCRR §766.1(c).
The person designated by the governing authority to oversee HIPAA compliance: [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME].

procedures: The governing authority designates a Privacy Officer, named in the HIPAA section of this manual, and a security contact for electronic systems. The Administrator reviews both designations at least annually.

Before the first service, the intake coordinator or RN gives the patient (or representative) the HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices and the written patient rights information. The rights information includes the rights to privacy, confidential records and refusal of release. The patient or representative signs an acknowledgment, which is filed in the clinical record. If the patient will not sign, the staff member documents the attempt and the reason.

The RN or intake coordinator explains in plain language, in the patient's preferred language (see CR-06), that records will not be released to any outside agency without written authorization except as the law permits. The staff member also explains that the patient may refuse release.

Before any release that is not permitted by law without authorization, the Privacy Officer or designee obtains a signed authorization. The authorization names the recipient, the information, the purpose and an expiration date, and states the patient's right to revoke. A copy goes to the patient and the original to the clinical record.

If the patient refuses to authorize a release, staff record the refusal in the record and release nothing. Staff tell the patient that care will continue unchanged. If a payer requires the information to authorize services, the RN explains the effect on payment (see CR-02) and the patient decides.

Disclosures permitted without authorization are limited to treatment, payment and health care operations, disclosures to NYS DOH and other government agencies when required by law, and other disclosures required by law. Each such disclosure is limited to the minimum necessary. The Privacy Officer approves any request that is not routine and logs it.

For a patient lacking capacity, the legally authorized representative signs authorizations and exercises privacy rights. Staff verify and document the representative's authority in the record before accepting a signature.

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets in the office. Only staff with a work need may access them. Patient records are not removed from the office except as the RN Director approves for care purposes, and they are signed out and back in on a record-removal log. Aides carry only the care plan and activity sheets for the assigned patient.

Electronic records are protected with unique user IDs, role-based access, strong passwords with multi-factor authentication where available, automatic log-off, encryption of laptops, phones and backups, and regular backups. The Administrator confirms that any electronic record can be printed on request, including for DOH.

Staff do not discuss patients in public places, on social media or with anyone without a work need. They do not text or email PHI except through agency-approved secure methods. Personal devices may be used for EVV or messaging only as SVC-13 and agency IT rules allow.

The agency enters into a written business associate agreement with any vendor or contractor that creates, receives or maintains PHI for the agency (see GOV-06). The Privacy Officer keeps the agreements on file.

The agency acts on patient requests to see or copy their record, to request an amendment and to receive an accounting of disclosures within the HIPAA time limits, generally 30 days. The Privacy Officer logs each request and the response.

All staff receive privacy and HIPAA training at hire, before patient contact, and again every year (see PER-05). The staff member signs a confidentiality agreement at hire. Training dates and content are filed in the personnel record.

Any staff member who suspects a privacy incident (lost record, misdirected message, stolen device, unauthorized access) reports it to the Privacy Officer immediately and no later than the end of the shift, and does not try to correct it alone. The Privacy Officer opens an incident file.

The Privacy Officer completes a documented breach risk assessment promptly. If a breach of unsecured PHI occurred, the agency notifies each affected patient in writing without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery. It reports the breach to HHS as HIPAA requires, and notifies the media where HIPAA requires it. Records of the assessment and notices are retained.

The agency takes corrective action after any breach, including retraining, security changes and discipline under PER-10. Staff are never retaliated against for good-faith reporting. Breach trends are reported to the QI Committee (see GOV-04).

The Privacy Officer reviews this policy and the NPP at least annually and when the law changes. Revised notices are given to current patients as required and a copy is filed in the policy manual (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, designates the Privacy Officer and ensures resources for safeguards.
Ensures systems, training and sanctions are in place and reviews breach reports.
Manages authorizations, requests, accounting of disclosures, breach assessment and notification, and annual review.
Explain privacy rights and the right to refuse release, obtain acknowledgments, and control record removal.
Keep PHI confidential, report incidents immediately and complete training.

documentation: Signed NPP acknowledgment and rights acknowledgment in the clinical record
Signed authorizations and documented refusals to release
Disclosure and accounting log; record-removal log
Business associate agreements
Staff confidentiality agreements and training records
Breach incident files, risk assessments and notices
Annual policy review record

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, nurses, supervisors, office staff, contractors and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect clients from financial exploitation and loss of property, to keep staff relationships with clients professional, and to set clear rules on gifts, money and client belongings.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] staff may not accept gifts, loans, bequests or money from clients or their families, and may not benefit financially from a client in any way. Caregivers may not handle client cash, credit or debit cards, checks or bank accounts, except for documented, authorized errands supported by receipts. Caregivers may not borrow from clients, sell anything to them or use client property for their own purposes. Any suspected exploitation is reported to the RN Director immediately. Clients have the right to be treated with respect and to complain without reprisal (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(10) and (a)(7)-(9)), and this policy supports those rights. Personnel policies, including conduct rules and job descriptions, are written and reviewed at least annually (10 NYCRR §766.11(a), (j)). The governing authority is responsible for compliance with all laws and for adopting policies (10 NYCRR §766.9(a)-(b), (d)). Violations lead to discipline up to termination and, where appropriate, referral to law enforcement and other authorities.

definitions.definition: Anything of value offered to staff by a client or family member, including cash, checks, jewelry, property, meals beyond routine hospitality, services, bequests and loans.

Improper use of a client's money, property or assets by another person, including theft, coercion, misuse of accounts or powers of attorney, and persuading a client to give, lend or leave money or property.
A shopping or similar errand for the client that is listed in the plan of care and aide care plan, approved by the RN, and documented with a receipt and a cash accounting.
Any item belonging to a client, including cash, cards, jewelry, medications, documents, mail, electronics, vehicles and household goods.

procedures: At hire and annually, every staff member is trained on this policy and signs an acknowledgment that they will not accept gifts, loans, bequests or money and will not borrow from, sell to or use the property of clients. The signed form is filed in the personnel record.

At admission, the RN or intake coordinator tells the client and family in plain language that staff cannot accept gifts or tips and may not handle money beyond authorized errands. This information is included in the written patient rights information (see CR-01).

If a client or family member offers a gift, the caregiver politely declines. A thank-you card or verbal thanks is acceptable. The caregiver reports the offer to the RN Director the same day if it involved money, valuables or repeated offers. The RN Director documents it.

If a gift cannot be returned safely or the client is distressed, the caregiver does not take the item and tells the RN Director. The RN Director or Administrator contacts the client or family and returns the item or explains the policy.

Any gift, bequest, loan, change of beneficiary, power of attorney, will witnessing or add-on to a joint account involving a staff member is prohibited. Staff must refuse and report immediately. The Administrator reviews every such report.

A shopping or other errand involving client funds is performed only if the plan of care and aide care plan authorize it and the RN has approved the arrangement (see SVC-06 and SVC-08). The RN documents the client's consent.

For an authorized errand, the caregiver and client count the cash together before and after. The caregiver keeps all receipts and returns exact change. Both sign the errand log or activity sheet. The caregiver uses their own funds only if the agency has expressly approved it, and never lends or borrows money.

Caregivers never use a client's credit or debit card, PIN, checks or online banking, never keep a client's card or PIN, and never take cash or valuables to their home. A client may not sign checks, cards or authorizations for the caregiver.

Caregivers do not use client property (car, phone, computer, food, supplies) for personal use. Use of a client's vehicle is governed by SAF-08. Caregivers do not sell, solicit or promote products, services, fundraisers or personal causes to clients.

At the initial RN assessment, the RN notes with the client any valuables the client wants kept secure and advises the client to secure cash, jewelry and important documents. The caregiver does not take responsibility for storing them.

A staff member who suspects that a client is being exploited by anyone (staff, family, friend or other) reports it immediately to the RN Director, by phone if necessary, and documents factual observations. Staff do not confront the suspected person or investigate on their own.

The RN Director notifies the Administrator immediately, takes steps to protect the client, and follows SAF-01 and SAF-02 for reporting to authorities and DOH. If a crime is in progress or a client is in danger, staff call 911.

When a client reports missing property, the RN Director takes a written report, asks the client to look for it, and notifies the Administrator within 24 hours. A staff member is removed from the case pending review where appropriate. Reports of suspected theft are referred to law enforcement.

The Administrator investigates, interviews involved staff and documents findings and any corrective action. The client or representative is told the outcome. Complaints of this kind are also logged under CR-03.
A substantiated violation results in disciplinary action up to termination (see PER-10). Where required, the agency also reports to the Home Care Worker Registry, licensing bodies or law enforcement.
Staff who report suspected exploitation in good faith are protected from retaliation. Retaliation is a separate ground for discipline.
The QI Committee reviews exploitation, property loss and gift reports at least quarterly (see GOV-04). The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and ensures compliance and annual review.
Investigates reports, determines discipline and external reporting, and protects reporters from retaliation.
Receives immediate reports, protects the client, approves errands and documents gift offers.
Decline gifts, follow errand rules, never handle client cards or accounts, and report suspicion immediately.
Explain the policy to clients and families at admission.

documentation: Signed staff acknowledgments of this policy
Gift offer reports and RN Director notes
Errand logs, receipts and signed cash accounting
Missing property and suspected exploitation reports and investigation files
Disciplinary records and external report copies
QI Committee review of these reports

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All staff, contractors and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], especially intake, nursing, scheduling and aide staff
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d)
policies.purpose: To make sure every patient is accepted and served without discrimination, that patients with limited English proficiency or disabilities can understand and use the agency's services and rights information, and that language preferences are recorded.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts and serves patients without discrimination on the basis of race, color, national origin, disability, age, sex, religion or payer source. This policy meets Applicant Worksheet p.5 item WS-ADM.2 — that patients are accepted without discrimination. Acceptance depends on a written, nondiscriminatory determination that the agency can safely and adequately meet the patient's assessed needs under its written admission criteria (10 NYCRR §766.9(i); see SVC-02). The agency also operates under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d) and the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101 et seq.). The agency provides interpreters and translated rights notices at no charge, makes reasonable accommodations for disability, and records the patient's language preference in the intake record. Patients receive their rights in writing before care begins (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(1)) and are treated with respect (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(10)), and these rights are delivered in a form the patient can understand. The governing authority is responsible for compliance with all applicable laws (10 NYCRR §766.9(a)-(b)).

definitions.definition: A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to take part in care without language help.

A trained person who is fluent in both English and the patient's language and can interpret accurately and impartially. A family member or minor child is not used except at the patient's informed request and when no safer option exists in an emergency.
A modification or aid that allows a person with a disability to take part in and benefit from services, unless it would fundamentally alter the service or impose an undue burden.
The method by which services are paid for (private pay, Medicaid, MLTC plan, insurance or other). Payer source is not used to discriminate in acceptance of a patient the agency is able to serve.

procedures: The Administrator ensures that the written admission criteria (see SVC-02) contain no criteria based on race, color, national origin, disability, age, sex, religion or payer source. The governing authority reviews the criteria at least annually.

At first contact, the intake coordinator asks and records in the intake record the patient's preferred spoken and written language, any need for an interpreter, and any communication need (hearing, vision, speech, literacy or cognitive).

If the patient or representative needs language help, the intake coordinator arranges a qualified interpreter (staff interpreter, contracted interpreter or telephone/video interpreter service) before assessment. The agency provides this at no charge to the patient. The interpreter's name or ID is documented in the record.

The agency does not require or ask the patient to provide their own interpreter. If a patient chooses to use a family member, the RN documents that the offer of a free interpreter was made and declined and that the choice was voluntary.

The agency provides the patient rights notice, statement of services and charges, grievance information and the HIPAA notice in the patient's language, using translated versions (see CR-01, CR-02, CR-03, CR-04). If a translation is not available, the RN uses an interpreter for sight translation, documents it, and the Administrator arranges a written translation promptly.

For patients with vision, hearing, speech or literacy needs, the staff member provides appropriate aids such as large print, reading the notice aloud, written materials, a sign-language interpreter, TTY or relay services. The aid provided is documented.

When a patient requests a reasonable accommodation, the RN Director decides with the patient, documents the accommodation in the plan of care and notifies the aide and scheduler. The accommodation is reviewed at each RN reassessment (see SVC-05).

Scheduling staff match aides to patients whose language fits the patient's needs whenever possible. Where no bilingual aide is available, the RN Director arranges interpreter support for the RN supervision and care plan orientation (see SVC-08).

Decisions to accept, decline, refer or discharge are made only on the basis of the agency's ability to meet assessed needs, licensed counties, staffing capacity and the criteria in SVC-02. The RN or Administrator documents the reason in writing for every declined referral.

Staff may not make any remark or take any action that treats a patient less favorably or harasses a patient because of a protected characteristic. A patient or staff member who believes discrimination has occurred reports it to the Administrator, who treats it as a grievance under CR-03. The patient is told they may also complain to DOH and to civil rights authorities.
The agency does not retaliate against any patient or staff member who raises a discrimination concern, and no patient is refused service for filing a complaint.

Staff are trained at orientation and annually on nondiscrimination, working with interpreters, disability accommodation and cultural humility (see PER-05). Completion is documented in the personnel record.
The Administrator posts or distributes a notice of nondiscrimination and language assistance in the office and with the rights packet, in the principal languages of the agency's service area.

The QI Committee reviews a summary of declined referrals, interpreter use, accommodation requests and discrimination complaints at least quarterly (see GOV-04). The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts nondiscriminatory criteria and ensures resources for interpreters and translation.
Contracts for interpreter services, posts notices, handles discrimination complaints and reviews declined referrals.
Records language preference and communication needs and arranges interpreters before assessment.
Make nondiscriminatory acceptance decisions, document accommodations and use interpreters for assessment and supervision.
Considers language and accommodation needs in aide assignments.
Treat all patients with respect and report any suspected discrimination.

documentation: Language preference and communication needs in the intake record
Interpreter use records (name or ID, date and mode)
Translated notices given and acknowledgments signed
Accommodation requests and responses in the plan of care
Written reasons for declined or referred-out referrals
Discrimination complaints and outcomes in the complaint log
Staff training records

policies.title: Personal Care Aide Duties, Scope of Tasks and What Caregivers May and May Not Do
policies.applies_to: Personal care aides (PCAs), RNs who assign and supervise aides, schedulers and the RN Director of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To define the duties and responsibilities of the personal care aide, set the scope of tasks aides may and may not perform, and require a practitioner's order and written plans before aides provide care.
policies.policy: This policy is the Personal Care Aide (PCA) policy and procedure of [AGENCY NAME] and meets Applicant Worksheet p.2 item WS-PCA.1 — the duties and responsibilities of the PCA — as described in the Procedures and Responsibilities sections below. The agency is a licensed home care services agency under PHL Article 36 (10 NYCRR §700.2). This policy also meets item WS-PCA.2 — scope of task. Level I covers nutritional and environmental support tasks only and is authorized for no more than 8 hours a week (18 NYCRR §505.14(a)(5)(i)). Level II adds personal care functions such as bathing, toileting, dressing and feeding, plus medication prompting and assistance but not administration (18 NYCRR §505.14(a)(5)(ii)). Aides may not perform nursing tasks or injections. This policy also meets item WS-PCA.3 — the need for a physician's order. Aides provide care only under a written order from an authorized practitioner. For Medicaid personal care, the order must come from a qualified independent practitioner, and care must be based on assessment, delivered under a plan of care and supervised by an RN (18 NYCRR §505.14(a)(1)). Aides work only from the written plan of care and the aide care plan, and supervision of aides is provided by an RN as appropriate (10 NYCRR §766.5(c)). The agency does not assign advanced home health aide tasks. Patients and workers may refuse advanced home health aide tasks, and no one is penalized for refusing (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(12)).

definitions.definition: An aide who meets the PCA qualifications and training in 10 NYCRR §700.2 and PER-02 and provides Level I and Level II personal care under RN supervision.
Nutritional and environmental support functions only (such as housekeeping, laundry, shopping and meal preparation), authorized for no more than 8 hours a week.
Level I tasks plus personal care functions such as bathing, toileting, dressing, feeding, transfer and ambulation help, and medication prompting and assistance, but not administration.
The tasks an aide is permitted, trained and authorized to perform for a particular patient as listed in the plan of care and aide care plan.

Reminding a patient to take medication and helping with opening containers or handing over pre-set medication when the patient self-directs, without deciding on, selecting, dosing or giving it (see SVC-11).
The practitioner licensed in New York who writes the medical order. For Medicaid personal care, the order comes from a qualified independent practitioner as 18 NYCRR §505.14 requires.
The written instructions for the aide, drawn from the plan of care, listing tasks, frequency, precautions and what to observe and report (see SVC-08).

procedures: The aide's duties and responsibilities are written in the PCA job description and given to each aide at hire (see PER-01). They include: perform only assigned tasks as written; arrive on time; use EVV; observe and report changes; document each visit; maintain client dignity, privacy and confidentiality; follow infection control; and follow abuse and incident reporting rules.

Before a patient is accepted, the RN confirms that a written order from an authorized practitioner exists. For Medicaid personal care, the RN also confirms that the order is from a qualified independent practitioner and that the plan or district has authorized services (see SVC-03 and SVC-07). No aide starts service without the order and authorization on file.

The RN builds the plan of care from the assessment (see SVC-05 and SVC-06) and writes the aide care plan listing each authorized task, frequency, and any precautions, diet, and limits. The aide care plan states whether the patient is authorized for Level I or Level II tasks.

For Level I patients, the RN assigns only nutritional and environmental support tasks. The scheduler does not schedule more than 8 hours a week of Level I service, and the RN reviews any request for more with the plan or district.

For Level II patients, the RN assigns the authorized personal care functions, such as bathing, toileting, dressing and feeding, as the plan specifies. Each task is within the aide's documented training. If the aide is not trained for a task, the RN trains and tests the aide (return demonstration) before the aide performs it, as in SVC-10.

Medication tasks are limited to prompting and assistance as the plan allows and the patient self-directs. Aides never administer medications, select or change doses, prepare injections, or decide what the patient should take (see SVC-11).

Aides may not perform nursing tasks, including injections, sterile or wound care, catheter or ostomy care beyond what the RN has trained and approved in writing within the aide scope, tube feedings, oxygen titration, or assessment of clinical status. The aide reports needs for such care to the RN, who arranges appropriate licensed care.

Before the first visit, an RN or a person under RN direction orients the aide to the plan of care and aide care plan, shows the aide where tasks are listed and records the orientation (see SVC-08). In-home RN supervision occurs at the initial service visit or on a change in aide, if the aide lacks documented training and experience in the tasks, and includes return demonstration (10 NYCRR §766.5(d)).

The RN supervises aides as appropriate, with the schedule in SVC-09 and SVC-10. RN in-home visits also occur on a change in condition to evaluate and revise the plan, and to instruct the aide in the observations and written reports required (10 NYCRR §766.5(d)).

If a patient or family asks an aide to do something outside the written plan, the aide politely declines, explains it is not in the plan and contacts the RN Director the same day. The RN Director decides whether the plan needs a change or not. Aides may not do extra tasks, even if the patient offers payment.

Advanced home health aide tasks are not assigned to aides. If the agency's license later includes advanced home health aide services (see GOV-09), the RN gives patients and workers the right to refuse such tasks and documents any refusal without penalty.
The aide documents each task on the activity sheet at each visit, reports any change in condition immediately to the RN, and does not leave a patient unsafe (see SVC-14).

The RN Director audits aide documentation and compares tasks performed with the plan at least during each supervisory visit. Variance (tasks not in the plan, tasks missed) is corrected through retraining. Repeated violations are managed under PER-10.

Scope-of-task and order requirements are covered in orientation and annual in-service training (see PER-05). The aide signs a statement acknowledging scope limits. The RN Director reviews this policy at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Perform only tasks in the plan of care and aide care plan, document each visit, report changes and decline tasks outside the scope.
Confirm the order and authorization, write the plan and aide care plan, assign aides by training and skill, train and supervise aides, and decide on any scope question.
Schedule only authorized hours and levels and assign aides as the RN directs.
Ensures sufficient trained supervisory staff and enforces scope-of-task rules.
Provides the order for services and any updates.

documentation: Practitioner order (and, for Medicaid, the independent practitioner order and authorization) in the clinical record
Plan of care and aide care plan listing tasks and level
Aide orientation record and return-demonstration documentation
Aide activity sheets and task documentation
RN supervisory visit reports
Aide acknowledgment of scope limits and training records
Variance and retraining records

policies.title: Admission Criteria, Acceptance of Patients and Informed Consent
policies.applies_to: The governing authority, Administrator, RN Director, RNs and intake staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set written admission criteria and a consistent process for accepting patients, so the agency accepts only patients whose needs it can safely and adequately meet, without discrimination, and with informed consent.
policies.policy: This is the Admissions policy and procedure of [AGENCY NAME] and meets Applicant Worksheet p.5 item WS-ADM.1 — admission criteria. The governing authority adopts and maintains written criteria for accepting patients (10 NYCRR §766.9(i)), listed in the Procedures. The agency meets item WS-ADM.2 — patients are accepted without discrimination (see CR-06). It meets item WS-ADM.3 — patient acceptance is based on the agency's ability to provide care consistent with the patient's assessed needs. It meets item WS-ADM.4 — patient needs can be met safely and adequately by the agency: a patient is accepted only after an RN, or a person directly supervised by an RN, determines that the agency can safely and adequately meet the patient's needs (10 NYCRR §766.3(a)). It meets Applicant Worksheet p.8 item WS-GA.11 — the agency accepts only patients to whom it can provide safe and adequate services (10 NYCRR §766.9(i)). It meets item WS-ADM.7 — informed consent: the patient or legally authorized representative gives informed consent before the first service. The patient receives the written rights notice and the statement of services and charges before care starts (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(1)-(3)). The agency declines or refers out when needs exceed its capacity or staffing.

definitions.definition: The written conditions, adopted by the governing authority, that a referral must meet to be accepted.

The patient's (or legally authorized representative's) voluntary, written agreement to receive services, given after the agency explains the services, who will provide them, charges, payer responsibility, the patient's rights and the right to refuse.
The care needs identified by the RN's professional assessment, and for Medicaid patients also by the independent assessment and authorization.
A person with legal authority to make decisions for a patient who lacks capacity, who exercises the patient's rights (10 NYCRR §766.1(c)).
Helping a person who cannot be accepted find another provider, with a written explanation.

procedures: Admission criteria. A referral is considered for acceptance when: (a) the person lives in a county covered by the agency's license; (b) the services needed fall within the agency's licensed services and aide scope (see SVC-01); (c) there is a written order from an authorized practitioner and, for Medicaid, a plan or district authorization (see SVC-03, SVC-07); (d) an RN has determined that the agency can safely and adequately meet the assessed needs; (e) the agency has trained staff available at the needed times; (f) the home environment is safe enough for care to be given (see SAF-07); and (g) payment arrangements are in place (see CR-02). The governing authority reviews these criteria at least annually.

The intake coordinator records every referral on an intake form, including date, source, name, address, contact, payer, language preference, requested services and urgency. Every referral is responded to within one business day.
No referral is declined or accepted on the basis of race, color, national origin, disability, age, sex, religion or payer source (see CR-06). The Administrator reviews every declined referral.

The intake coordinator gathers the order, authorization and referral information and sends them to an RN. An RN, or a person directly supervised by an RN, evaluates whether the agency can safely and adequately meet the patient's needs (10 NYCRR §766.3(a)). The evaluation addresses clinical needs, supervision needs, home safety, available staffing, schedule, language and equipment.
The RN completes the professional assessment as described in SVC-05, and for Medicaid patients also uses the independent assessment information under SVC-03.

The RN documents the acceptance decision on the admission determination form: the findings, the services accepted, and the signature, title and date of the RN (or the supervised person and the RN who approved).

If the RN determines the agency can meet the needs, the intake coordinator schedules the admission visit. The agency may not start services until the order, authorization (if Medicaid) and RN determination are on file.

Before the first service, the RN or authorized staff member gives the patient or representative, in a language they understand (see CR-06), the written patient rights, a statement of services and charges, and an explanation of what the third-party payer is expected to pay and what the patient must pay (see CR-01, CR-02). The patient signs an acknowledgment, which is filed in the clinical record.

The RN explains, and answers questions about, the services to be provided and who will provide them; the plan of care; the patient's right to take part in planning care and to refuse care; how to complain, including to DOH; privacy practices; and the agency's discharge policies (see SVC-15). The RN checks the patient's understanding.
