Notices to MLTC plan or district and referral records
Discharge summary in the clinical record
Quarterly discharge review for the QI Committee

policies.title: Palliative Care and Life-Limiting Illness
policies.applies_to: RN Director, supervising RNs, intake staff, personal care aides and all care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure patients of [AGENCY NAME] who have a life-limiting condition or illness are offered information and counseling, can reach palliative care consultation and services (including pain management) by referral, have their palliative needs written into the plan of care, and are protected when they cannot make decisions for themselves.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will identify patients with life-limiting conditions and illnesses, and will give them and their families or representatives information and counseling suited to their condition and wishes. This policy meets Applicant Worksheet p.8 item WS-PAL.1 (Palliative Care policy/procedure: access to information and counseling appropriate to patients with life-limiting conditions and illnesses). Agency nurses do not provide palliative medical treatment on their own authority. The agency gives patients access to palliative care consultation and services, including pain management, by referring them to the authorized practitioner and to community palliative care or hospice providers. This policy meets item WS-PAL.2 (access to palliative care consultation and services including pain management). Palliative care needs are identified in the RN assessment and recorded in the plan of care, which is reviewed as often as needed and at least every six months (10 NYCRR §766.3(b), (d)(1)). Patients keep the rights to take part in care planning and to refuse care (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(5)-(6)). When a patient lacks capacity to make decisions, a legally authorized representative or health care proxy receives the information and makes the decisions, as 10 NYCRR §766.1(c) provides. This policy meets item WS-PAL.3 (patients who lack capacity to make decisions). The agency accepts and keeps a patient only while the RN determines that the agency can safely and adequately meet the patient's needs (10 NYCRR §766.3(a)). When needs exceed the agency's scope, the agency follows SVC-15 for transfer and discharge planning.

definitions.definition: A condition or illness, such as advanced cancer, end-stage heart, lung, kidney or liver disease, or advanced dementia, that is expected to shorten life or that the practitioner, patient or family considers to be in an advanced stage.

Care that focuses on relieving pain and other symptoms and on the comfort, dignity and quality of life of the patient and family, and that may be given alongside treatment meant to cure or control the illness.
A separately licensed or certified program that provides comfort-focused care to patients near the end of life. The agency refers to hospice but does not provide it under this license.
The physician, nurse practitioner or other practitioner authorized to order care for the patient, who is named in the clinical record.

definitions.term: Legally authorized representative / health care proxy
definitions.definition: The person with legal authority to decide for a patient who lacks capacity, such as an agent named in a health care proxy or another person with legal authority under New York law.

procedures: At intake and at every RN assessment and reassessment, the RN asks about the patient's diagnoses, prognosis, symptoms (especially pain, breathlessness, nausea, anxiety and fatigue), goals of care and wishes for care at the end of life. The RN documents the answers in the assessment.

The RN flags the patient in the clinical record as having a life-limiting condition or illness when any of these apply: the practitioner says so, the diagnosis is advanced or end-stage, the patient or family reports it, or the patient's function is declining quickly.

Within the same visit or no later than 2 business days after the flag is set, the RN offers the patient and family (or representative) information and counseling in plain language and the patient's preferred language (see CR-06). Topics are the illness and what to expect, comfort and symptom management, palliative care and hospice options, advance care planning, and the services the agency can and cannot provide.

The RN gives the patient written information on palliative care and hospice, a list of local palliative care and hospice providers, and the agency phone number for the RN on call. The RN documents what was offered and what the patient accepted or declined.

The RN asks whether the patient has a health care proxy, living will, MOLST or do-not-resuscitate order or similar document. If the patient has one, the RN asks for a copy for the clinical record and notes where the original is kept. If the patient has none, the RN offers general information and refers questions about forms to the practitioner. The RN does not give legal advice.

When the patient has uncontrolled pain or other symptoms, or asks for palliative care, the RN contacts the authorized practitioner the same day, reports the findings and asks for orders or a referral for palliative care consultation, pain management, or hospice evaluation. The RN documents the call, the response and any order (see SVC-07).

The RN makes the referral in writing or by phone to the palliative care or hospice provider the patient chooses. The RN sends the information that provider needs, with the patient's consent, and documents the referral date, who accepted it and the outcome. The agency does not steer a patient to a particular provider.

The RN adds the patient's palliative care needs and goals to the plan of care: symptom management goals, the practitioner's pain-management orders, comfort measures for aides, advance directive status, and who is to be called for what. The plan is reviewed with the patient or representative and revised promptly when needs change, and at least every six months (see SVC-06). Where the patient's care is authorized by an MLTC plan, the RN also tells the plan's care manager about the change in needs (see SVC-17).

The RN gives the aide a care plan that matches the plan of care and explains comfort tasks, positioning, skin care, and signs that must be reported (see SVC-08). Aides do not give or adjust pain medication beyond the assistance allowed in SVC-11. They report any pain, distress or change in condition to the RN the same day.

The RN monitors the patient at least as often as the plan of care and supervisory schedule require. The RN follows up on each pain or symptom report, checks the effect of any change the practitioner ordered, and alerts the practitioner promptly to significant changes in condition (10 NYCRR §766.3(d)(2); see SVC-14).

At the time of assessment, the RN decides whether the patient has capacity to understand information and make decisions about care. The RN uses the practitioner's findings where available and documents the basis for the decision. Capacity is assumed unless there is a reason to doubt it. A patient may have capacity for some decisions and not for others.

If the patient lacks capacity, the RN identifies the legally authorized representative or health care proxy agent and asks for a copy of the document or other proof of authority. The RN gives all required information and counseling to that person, involves the patient to the extent the patient can take part, and documents the person's name, relationship, contact details and authority in the clinical record.

The legally authorized representative exercises the patient's rights under 10 NYCRR §766.1(c), including consent to or refusal of care and participation in care planning. The RN documents each decision and the information given. If no representative can be identified, or if the family disagrees, the RN notifies the RN Director, who consults the practitioner and the Administrator and, if necessary, counsel or the ethics resource named in [ETHICS RESOURCE], before any change is made to care.

If a patient or representative asks to stop services or changes the goals of care, the RN documents the request, notifies the practitioner and the payer, revises the plan of care and, if services are to end, follows SVC-15. A refusal of one service does not take away the patient's right to other services.

If a patient shows signs of dying, the RN reviews the advance directive status with the family, makes sure family and practitioner know who to call, and confirms who the on-call RN is. Aides call 911 only when emergency steps are called for in SVC-14 and tell the RN immediately. The RN then tells responders about any valid order the family produces.

After a patient dies, the RN documents the date, time and circumstances in the clinical record, notifies the practitioner and payer, completes the discharge summary, and offers the family information on bereavement support. The RN Director reviews the death in the next QI cycle if it raised any care concern (see GOV-04).

The RN Director gives all RNs and aides training on this policy at orientation and in annual in-service, including recognizing pain, comfort care and dignity, communicating with families, and what aides may and may not do (see PER-05 and SVC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, trains staff, reviews referrals and unresolved cases, and reports on palliative care referrals and outcomes to the QI committee.

Identifies palliative needs, gives information and counseling, contacts the practitioner, makes referrals, writes palliative needs into the plan of care, decides capacity and identifies the representative.
Follows the care plan, gives comfort and dignity care within scope, and reports pain, distress or change in condition to the RN the same day.
Tells the RN at referral when a life-limiting illness is mentioned and records any health care proxy or representative details provided.
Makes sure the RN Director has the time and resources to carry out the policy and resolves disputes that cannot be settled at RN level.

documentation: RN assessment documenting symptoms, prognosis, goals and capacity decision
Record of information and counseling given and written materials provided
Practitioner contact notes and orders, and referral records with dates and outcomes
Plan of care showing palliative needs and each review or revision
Copies of health care proxy, MOLST and other advance directives, or note that the patient has none
Name, authority and contact details of any legally authorized representative or health care proxy agent
Patient or representative decisions, refusals and changes in goals of care
Discharge summary or death note

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs, MLTC Plans and Payers
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN Director, intake and scheduling staff, billing staff and supervising RNs
policies.purpose: To make sure that care [AGENCY NAME] delivers to Medicaid and Managed Long Term Care (MLTC) patients matches what the plan or social services district authorized, that contract terms on rates, wages and billing are in writing, and that wage and minimum-needs rules are followed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] delivers Medicaid personal care only as authorized by the patient's MLTC plan or social services district. The plan remains responsible for authorizing services and for recording the level, amount, frequency and duration of authorized services in the plan of care with notice to the enrollee (DOH Medicaid Managed Care NYIA guidance). The agency's plan of care and aide care plan must match that authorization, and the agency does not provide more or fewer hours than authorized without a new authorization or a documented plan-approved exception. Personal care must be medically necessary, ordered by a qualified independent practitioner, based on assessment, delivered under a plan of care and supervised by an RN (18 NYCRR 505.14(a)(1)). The agency follows the Level I and Level II task limits in 18 NYCRR 505.14(a)(5) and the minimum needs requirements for adults 21 and over, effective 9/1/2025, in the DOH Minimum Needs Requirements. Each plan contract is put in writing and states rates, wage pass-through and billing terms. The agency pays the home care aide minimum wage under PHL §3614-f and, for Medicaid-funded care in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester, the wage parity benefit under PHL §3614-c. Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program (CDPAP) services are handled by the Statewide Fiscal Intermediary, not by this agency. Electronic visit verification for personal care is governed by 42 USC 1396b(l) and SVC-13.

definitions.definition: A Managed Long Term Care plan or other managed care organization that authorizes and pays for home care for its enrollees and contracts with the agency.
The New York Independent Assessor, which carries out the independent assessment and practitioner order for Medicaid personal care and CDPAP, in coordination with the plan.
The written approval from the plan or social services district stating the level, amount, frequency and duration of services the agency may provide and bill.

definitions.term: Level I / Level II personal care
definitions.definition: Level I is nutritional and environmental support tasks only, authorized for no more than 8 hours a week. Level II adds personal care functions, including medication prompting and assistance but not administration (18 NYCRR 505.14(a)(5)).
The total compensation requirement for Medicaid-funded home care aides in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester under PHL §3614-c.
Public Partnerships LLC (PPL), the single entity that serves as fiscal intermediary for CDPAP.

procedures: Before the agency signs a plan contract, the Administrator reviews it for rates, authorization process, billing and payment terms, wage pass-through, reporting duties, record access, audit rights, termination rights and any limit on enrollees. The Administrator has counsel review the contract as needed. Final signed contracts are kept under GOV-06.

The Administrator confirms and documents each plan's contract limit before expecting referrals. MLTC plans may contract with no more than 1 LHCSA per 100 enrollees downstate or per 60 enrollees in the rest of the state, with at least two LHCSAs per county accepting new enrollees. If the agency needs an exception, the Administrator emails LHCSAExceptions@health.ny.gov and keeps the correspondence.

The Administrator obtains in writing, for each plan, the hourly or visit rates, the portion of the rate designated for aide wages and benefits, how that pass-through is reported, invoice requirements and payment timeframes. Any rate or term change is accepted only in writing and is filed with the contract.

When a referral arrives, intake staff record the referral source, plan name, enrollee ID, authorization number, authorized service level, hours, frequency, duration and start date, and verify the authorization in the plan's portal or in writing. No service starts without a verified authorization, except where the contract states a written exception.

The RN Director or designee confirms that the patient meets the minimum needs requirements as determined by the independent assessment, and does not accept a referral that does not match the authorization. For adults 21 and over, that means limited assistance with more than two ADLs, or supervision with more than one ADL for dementia or Alzheimer's (18 NYCRR 505.14(a)(3)(iv); DOH Minimum Needs Requirements, effective 9/1/2025). The agency does not itself determine eligibility. If the paperwork does not show that the requirement is met, the agency asks the plan for clarification before service starts (see SVC-03).

The assessing RN carries out the agency's RN assessment (see SVC-05) and writes the plan of care so that the level, amount, frequency and duration match the authorization. Where the authorization is Level I, the plan lists only Level I tasks. Where the authorization is Level II, the plan lists the Level II functions the patient needs. The RN documents the authorization number and dates in the plan of care.

If the RN finds the authorized services are not enough or are too much for the patient's needs, the RN notifies the plan's care manager in writing within 2 business days, with the clinical reasons, and asks for reassessment or revised authorization. The agency keeps providing the authorized service in the meantime, unless the patient's safety requires an emergency step under SVC-14.

For live-in 24-hour or continuous personal care, the RN Director confirms the authorization states the arrangement. For live-in care, the RN confirms that the aide's sleep is likely to be uninterrupted for 5 hours. For continuous care, the RN confirms that the authorization covers more than 16 hours a day by more than one aide (18 NYCRR 505.14(a)(2), (4)). For any authorization of more than 12 hours a day on average, the RN confirms the additional documentation required by 18 NYCRR 505.14(a)(5)(ii)(b) has been supplied by the authorizing entity.

Scheduling staff schedule aides only for authorized hours and tasks. Any request by a patient or family for more hours, or for tasks outside the authorization, is sent to the RN, who refers it to the plan. The agency does not provide the extra service free of charge as an inducement. Private-pay hours beyond the authorization may be offered only under a separate written service agreement under CR-02 and must be kept separate in the records.

Aides record each visit in the electronic visit verification system under SVC-13. Billing staff bill only for visits that match the authorization and the verified visit records, in line with GOV-05. Billing staff reconcile each plan invoice with authorization, visit records and aide timekeeping before submission and correct any mismatch first.

The RN Director schedules reassessments and plan of care reviews with the plan's authorization dates in mind, tracks upcoming expirations, and starts the reauthorization request or contacts the plan's care manager at least 30 days before each authorization ends (or sooner if the plan requires). The agency also notifies the plan of hospitalizations, deaths, discharges, refusals of care and significant changes in condition under SVC-14 and SVC-15.

For patients who ask about CDPAP, intake staff explain that CDPAP is provided through the Statewide Fiscal Intermediary (PPL) and not through this agency. Staff give the patient the plan's or the Fiscal Intermediary's contact details and do not enroll patients in CDPAP. The agency does not act as a CDPAP fiscal intermediary.

The Administrator and payroll staff pay all home care aides at least the home care aide minimum wage required by PHL §3614-f: $19.65 per hour in New York City, Long Island and Westchester and $18.65 per hour in the rest of the state as of 1/1/2026, rising to $20.00 and $19.00 on 1/1/2027. The Administrator updates payroll rates before each effective date and documents the change.

For Medicaid-funded home care in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester, payroll staff pay total compensation of the home care aide minimum plus the benefit portion required by PHL §3614-c: $2.54 per hour in New York City, and $1.67 per hour in Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester, from 1/1/2024. In 2026 total compensation is $22.19 in New York City and $21.32 in the other three counties. The agency provides the benefit portion as wages, benefits or both, and does not reduce it by any other payment.

The Administrator files the annual wage parity certification and obtains the independently audited statement required by PHL §3614-c, and keeps wage parity records for 10 years. Payroll records also follow PER-09. The Administrator reviews the compliance results with the QI committee at least annually.

Each month, the Administrator or billing lead reviews denials, recoupments, audits and plan requests, and reports to the Administrator and Compliance Officer. Any concern about billing for services not delivered, services not authorized, or inaccurate wage reporting is handled under GOV-05.

The Administrator keeps current contact information for each plan's care management, authorization, billing and provider relations staff and for the Department of Health offices named in GOV-07, and distributes it to the RN Director, intake and billing staff.

responsibilities.duty: Negotiates and signs plan contracts, confirms rates and wage pass-through terms in writing, manages contract limits and exception requests, and ensures wage and wage parity compliance.
Makes sure plans of care match authorizations, monitors minimum needs documentation, communicates clinical changes to plans, and tracks reauthorization dates.
Writes the plan of care to the authorization, reports mismatches in need, and alerts plan care managers to changes.
Verifies authorizations before service, records authorization details and refers CDPAP inquiries to the Statewide Fiscal Intermediary.
Schedules only authorized hours and tasks and flags requests outside the authorization.
Bill only verified, authorized visits, pay required minimum and parity wages, maintain 10-year wage parity records and prepare certification materials.
Reviews billing and wage compliance results and investigates concerns under GOV-05.

documentation: Signed plan contracts with rate, pass-through and billing terms
Contract-limit correspondence, including any exception requests to LHCSAExceptions@health.ny.gov
Authorization verification for each patient, with level, amount, frequency, duration and dates
Plan of care showing authorization match and minimum needs documentation
Communications with plan care managers about changes, reassessment and reauthorization
Verified visit records and reconciliations to invoices
Payroll records showing minimum wage and wage parity benefit amounts
Wage parity annual certification and independently audited statement (kept 10 years)
Monthly billing and denial review notes

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, aides, nurses, contractors, volunteers, administrators and governing authority members
policies.purpose: To protect patients of [AGENCY NAME] from abuse, neglect and exploitation by screening staff before hire, training staff to recognize and report concerns, requiring immediate reporting, and prohibiting retaliation.
policies.policy: Every patient has the right to be treated with respect and dignity and to be free from mistreatment (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(10)). [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect or exploitation of any patient by any person. All staff must report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the RN Director at once. Staff who see a client in immediate danger call 911 first. The RN Director reports to Adult Protective Services and law enforcement as required by law and keeps the statutory reporting citations approved by counsel in the compliance file at [ADDRESS]. Retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith, or against a patient who complains, is prohibited (10 NYCRR §766.1(a)(7)-(9)). The agency verifies each person's qualifications and registry information before hire (10 NYCRR §766.11(b)) and runs a criminal history record check on every prospective employee with the timelines in 10 NYCRR §402.6. Every report and its outcome is documented in the incident record and presented in the QI report.

definitions.definition: Any intentional or reckless act that causes or may cause physical, sexual, emotional or psychological harm to a patient, including hitting, restraining, sexual contact, threats, humiliation, isolation or withholding of needed items.
Failure to provide, or willful withholding of, care, supervision, food, hygiene or safety that a patient needs and that staff are responsible for providing, whether intentional or from carelessness.
Improper use of a patient's money, property, identity or resources for the benefit of someone else, including theft, forged signatures, coerced gifts, borrowing money or misuse of accounts and cards.
Any observation, statement or sign that would lead a reasonable person to think a patient may have been abused, neglected or exploited. Proof is not required before reporting.
The county or New York City social services unit that investigates reports of vulnerable adults who may be at risk and arranges protective help.

procedures: Before hire, the Administrator or designee verifies identity, employment history and references, and checks the Home Care Worker Registry information for each candidate, as described in PER-02, PER-03 and PER-08. The agency does not place an applicant with patients until these verifications are complete.

The designated agency representative submits the criminal history record check request for each prospective employee under PER-04. An authorized person signs the DOH form, and the form and two sets of fingerprints are sent to DOH within 10 business days of taking the prints. The applicant presents two forms of ID, one government-issued with signature and at least one with photo. If prints are rejected, the agency resubmits within 14 days of notice. Where temporary approval is used pending results, the person works only under the supervision the rule requires (10 NYCRR §402.6).

At orientation and in annual in-service, the RN Director trains all staff on this policy: types and signs of abuse, neglect and exploitation, how to report, protection from retaliation, professional boundaries (PER-10) and client property and gifts rules (CR-05). Attendance is documented in the personnel record.

At admission, the RN gives each patient and representative the written patient rights, including freedom from mistreatment and the right to complain without reprisal, and the phone numbers for the agency, the DOH complaint line and the RN Director (see CR-01 and CR-03).

Any staff member who sees, hears of or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation of a patient, whoever the alleged person is, reports it to the RN Director immediately by phone at [PHONE], or to the Administrator at [PHONE] if the RN Director is unavailable or involved. Staff do not wait for proof, do not investigate on their own and do not tell the alleged person they have reported.

If the patient is in immediate danger or needs urgent medical care, the staff member calls 911 first, stays with the patient if safe to do so, and then calls the RN Director. The RN Director or designee follows up under SVC-14.

The RN Director or designee goes to the home or contacts the patient the same day, if safe, to assess the patient, arrange medical care and ensure the patient's immediate safety. The RN Director removes the staff member involved from the patient's schedule and, as appropriate, from duty pending review.

The RN Director makes reports to Adult Protective Services and, where a crime is suspected, to law enforcement as required by law, and consults counsel where needed to confirm the reporting requirement and deadline. The RN Director records the date, time, person contacted and report number. The agency also tells the patient's practitioner, the legally authorized representative where appropriate, and the MLTC plan care manager (see SVC-17), and notifies DOH where required under REC-04.

The RN Director completes a written incident report the same day (see SAF-02) and opens an investigation. The investigation includes interviews of the patient, the staff involved and witnesses, review of schedules, visit records and notes, and a written finding within 14 days unless an outside agency requests that the agency wait.
The Administrator makes sure that the agency cooperates fully with APS, law enforcement and DOH investigators and gives them access to records as the law allows (see CR-04).

If the investigation substantiates abuse, neglect or exploitation by a staff member, the Administrator takes disciplinary action up to and including termination, and reports to licensing or certifying bodies and the Home Care Worker Registry as required (see PER-03). If a criminal history or other information shows a barred person is working, the Administrator removes the person from patient contact immediately.

The agency prohibits retaliation against any staff member who reports in good faith, against any patient or family who complains, and against anyone who takes part in an investigation. Any retaliation is itself misconduct subject to discipline. The Administrator reviews complaints of retaliation personally.

The RN Director gives the patient and the family a plan to protect the patient, including a change of aide and any safety measures, and follows up with the patient within 7 days and again at the next supervisory visit.

Staff who are mandated reporters under their own professional licenses understand that their individual reporting duties remain in force in addition to the agency's procedures. Reporting to the RN Director does not replace a personal duty to report where the law makes one.

The RN Director enters each report, finding and action in the incident log and the QI committee reviews summary data, trends and corrective actions at least quarterly, without patient names where not needed (see GOV-04).
The RN Director and Administrator review this policy at least annually and after any substantiated case, and revise training and screening where weaknesses are found.

responsibilities.duty: Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the RN Director at once, call 911 for immediate danger, and cooperate with investigations.
Receives reports, protects the patient, reports to APS and law enforcement as required, investigates, and tracks outcomes and training.
Ensures pre-hire checks, discipline, no retaliation, outside-agency cooperation and counsel review of statutory reporting requirements.
Completes identity, reference, Registry and criminal history record check steps before patient contact.
Reviews incident data and trends and recommends corrective actions.

documentation: Staff training attendance and acknowledgment records
Criminal history record check submissions, dates, ID verification and results
Registry check and reference verification records
Incident report and investigation file
Record of reports to APS, law enforcement, DOH, practitioner and plan
Disciplinary and retaliation review records
Incident log and QI committee summaries
Patient rights acknowledgment in the clinical record

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, aides, nurses, contractors, RN Director, Administrator and QI committee
policies.purpose: To make sure that every accident or incident involving a patient, staff member or visitor in the course of the agency's services is reported immediately, documented in the clinical record, reviewed, reported to those who must be told, and used to improve safety.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires staff to report every accident and incident to the RN Director immediately. The agency records accidents and incidents in the patient's clinical record, as 10 NYCRR §766.6(a)(8) requires. This policy meets Applicant Worksheet p.7 item WS-CR.13 (documentation of accidents/incidents). The RN Director files a written incident report within 24 hours after learning of the event. The agency notifies the practitioner, the family or representative, the MLTC plan and the Department of Health as required, and sends all incidents to the QI committee for review (10 NYCRR §766.9(k)-(l)). The agency gives DOH the records and reports it requires promptly (10 NYCRR §766.12(a)).

definitions.definition: An unexpected event that results in, or could have resulted in, injury or harm, such as a fall, burn, choking, or an injury to an aide while providing care.

Any event that is out of the ordinary and that affects or could affect the safety or well-being of a patient or staff member, including accidents, medication errors, suspected abuse or neglect, missing or damaged property, elopement, unexpected hospitalization, death, threats or violence, exposure to blood or body fluids, and a patient's refusal of needed care that creates risk.
An incident that causes death, serious injury or serious risk, which requires same-day review by the RN Director and Administrator.
An event that could have caused harm but did not, and which is reported so that causes can be corrected.

procedures: The staff member first makes the situation safe and gets help. For any injury or medical emergency, the staff member calls 911 where needed and follows SVC-14.

The staff member reports the event by phone to the RN Director at [PHONE] immediately. After hours, the staff member calls the on-call RN at [PHONE]. If the event involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member also follows SAF-01.

The RN Director or on-call RN determines whether the patient needs medical care or the patient's care needs have changed, instructs the staff member, and visits the home or contacts the patient the same day where the event involved harm, risk of harm or a change in condition.

The staff member writes a factual account of the event before the end of the shift, and no later than 24 hours after the event, on the agency incident form: who, what, when, where, what was seen and done, who was told and any witnesses. The account is limited to facts and does not blame or speculate.

The RN Director records the incident in the patient's clinical record under 10 NYCRR §766.6(a)(8): date, time, description, the patient's condition, actions taken, notifications made and follow-up. The RN also makes a progress note. For incidents involving staff injury only, the report goes to the personnel file and incident log, not the patient's clinical record, unless a patient was involved.
The RN Director files the completed written incident report in the incident log within 24 hours after learning of the event, and the Administrator is told of any sentinel event the same day.

The RN Director notifies the patient's authorized practitioner promptly of any incident that affects the patient's condition, plan of care or orders, and documents the call and response (see SVC-07 and SVC-14).

The RN Director notifies the patient's family or legally authorized representative on the same day, with the patient's permission where required by privacy law (see CR-04), unless it is not safe or possible, and documents the contact.
The RN Director notifies the MLTC plan care manager or other payer as required by the contract (see SVC-17) and within the time the contract sets, and documents the notice.

The Administrator decides with the RN Director whether the event must be reported to DOH or another agency, such as law enforcement, APS, the local health department or the Department of Labor. The Administrator uses the DOH reporting requirements and the Health Commerce System reporting process in GOV-07 and REC-04 and consults counsel where needed. The date, method and recipient of every report are recorded.

The RN Director investigates each incident to find causes and contributing factors: review the clinical record, interview those involved, check the plan of care and aide care plan, and examine equipment and home conditions. The RN Director finishes the review within 14 days and records findings and corrective actions on the incident form.

The RN Director carries out corrective actions, such as changes to the plan of care, extra training, a change of aide, equipment, referral for home safety evaluation or discipline, and records the date and the person responsible. The Administrator makes sure that corrective actions are carried out.
For medication-related incidents, including errors in prompting or assistance, the RN Director reviews the event under SVC-11 and determines whether the practitioner and plan must be told.
For any exposure to blood or body fluids, the exposed person also follows SAF-04. For any injury to staff, the Administrator makes sure a workers' compensation report is filed as required by law.

The RN Director summarizes all incidents each quarter by type, patient, staff, location, cause and outcome, and presents the summary to the QI committee. The committee reviews trends and recommends system improvements (see GOV-04). Incident data supports the committee's random sample review and the written summary sent to the governing authority.

Incident reports are kept as part of the clinical record when patient-related, and the incident log and QI records are kept as agency records for the periods required in REC-02 and REC-03. Electronic incident records are kept securely and can be printed on request (10 NYCRR §766.12(b)).

responsibilities.duty: Make the situation safe, report immediately to the RN Director, and write a factual report within 24 hours.
Directs response, documents in the clinical record, files the written report within 24 hours, notifies practitioner, family and plan, investigates and monitors corrective actions.
Decides on DOH and other external reporting, ensures corrective action, and reviews sentinel events.
Reviews incident trends each quarter and recommends improvements.

documentation: Staff incident report form with factual account
Clinical record entry under 10 NYCRR §766.6(a)(8) and progress note
Incident log with dates and tracking numbers
Records of notifications to practitioner, family, plan, DOH and others
Investigation findings and corrective action records
Quarterly incident summary and QI committee minutes

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All nurses, personal care aides, supervisors and any staff who enter patient homes or handle supplies and equipment
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among patients, families and staff of [AGENCY NAME] by applying Standard/Universal Precautions, hand hygiene, clean bag technique, proper cleaning and disinfection, reporting of communicable disease and control of occupational exposure.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] applies Standard/Universal Precautions with every patient, every time, whether or not the patient is known to have an infection. This policy meets Applicant Worksheet p.13 item WS-IC.1 (Infection Control policy/procedure: Universal Precautions/Standard Precautions). The procedures below are the agency's procedure to prevent the spread of infection and meet item WS-IC.2. Handwashing is taught and checked under Procedures 4-5 (WS-IC.3). Nurses are trained in nursing bag management and technique (WS-IC.4) and aides in home health aide bag technique (WS-IC.5), under Procedures 6-9. Reporting of communicable disease is covered in Procedures 14-15 (WS-IC.6). Occupational exposure control is addressed in Procedure 16 and in SAF-04 (WS-IC.7). The agency follows written procedures for the storage, cleaning and disinfection of supplies and equipment (10 NYCRR §766.2(a)(5)). Employee health requirements, immunization and TB screening are in PER-06 and PER-07 (10 NYCRR §766.11(c)-(d)). The bloodborne pathogen program is in SAF-04, consistent with 29 CFR 1910.1030.

definitions.definition: Infection prevention practices applied to all patients, treating blood, body fluids, non-intact skin and mucous membranes as possibly infectious. They include hand hygiene, gloves and other protective equipment, safe handling of sharps and soiled items, and cleaning and disinfection.
Gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection and similar barriers worn to prevent contact with infectious material.
A method of carrying, setting up, using and cleaning a work bag so that supplies stay clean and are not a source of cross-contamination between homes.
An illness that can be passed from one person to another and that may be reportable to the public health authorities under law.
Contact of a worker's skin, eyes, mouth or other mucous membrane with blood or other potentially infectious material while working.

procedures: The RN Director is responsible for this program. The RN Director gives every new nurse and aide training on Standard/Universal Precautions at orientation before patient contact and annually in in-service (see PER-05). Attendance and a competency check are documented in the personnel record.

Staff apply Standard/Universal Precautions with every patient. They treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, cover cuts with waterproof dressings, and do not eat, drink or apply cosmetics while giving care.

The RN assesses each patient and home at admission for infection risks (known infections, wounds, devices, immune status, household members who are ill, home sanitation, availability of water and soap) and records them in the assessment. The RN tells the aide the precautions required in the care plan (see SVC-08).

Hand hygiene: staff wash hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds when hands are visibly soiled, and use alcohol-based hand rub (at least 60% alcohol) when they are not. Staff clean their hands on arrival, before and after each patient contact, before putting on and after removing gloves, before preparing or handling food, after toileting or perineal care, after handling soiled linen or waste, after contact with blood or body fluids, and on leaving the home.
The RN observes and checks hand hygiene technique at orientation, at each supervisory visit (see SVC-10) and at the annual performance evaluation, and re-teaches and documents corrections.

Nursing bag technique: nurses keep supplies in a bag that can be wiped clean. They put the bag on a clean, dry, hard surface away from pets, children and soiled areas, and not on a floor, bed or soiled surface. They wash their hands before getting into the bag, remove only what is needed, never return used items to the bag, and keep clean and dirty items separate.

Nurses clean the outside of the nursing bag with an approved disinfectant at least weekly and when visibly soiled, and clean reusable equipment such as stethoscopes, thermometers and blood pressure cuffs with an approved disinfectant between patients. Single-use items are used once and discarded. Nurses do not carry items from one home to another that cannot be cleaned.

Home health aide bag technique: aides who carry an aide bag use it the same way. They put it on a clean surface, wash their hands before and after use, take out only what is needed, keep clean and used items apart, leave the bag clean and close it, and never leave it where children or pets can reach it. Aides clean the outside of the bag at least weekly and when soiled.

The agency provides aides and nurses with enough gloves, hand rub, disinfectant wipes, waste bags and other items to follow these procedures, at no cost to staff. Staff tell the supervisor when supplies run low.

Staff wear gloves when touching blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin or soiled items, and change them between tasks and patients. Staff wear gowns, masks or eye protection when splashes or sprays are likely, and follow the RN's added precautions where the patient has a specific infection. Staff remove PPE carefully, discard it in the proper waste bag and wash their hands.

Staff handle sharps only as allowed by their scope (see SVC-01 and SVC-11) and never recap, bend or break needles. Any sharps are placed in a puncture-resistant container, never in household trash. Staff teach patients and caregivers safe disposal of sharps.

Staff handle soiled linen and clothing as little as possible and without shaking it, bag it at the place of use, and wash it in hot water with detergent where available. Waste soaked with blood or body fluid is double-bagged and disposed of as the RN instructs and as local rules require.

Cleaning and disinfection of supplies and equipment: the RN Director keeps written procedures for storage, cleaning and disinfection of agency-owned supplies and equipment (10 NYCRR §766.2(a)(5)). They name the approved disinfectants, contact times, who cleans which item and how often, and how clean and used items are stored. Staff clean and disinfect shared equipment between patients and document it. Patient-owned equipment is cleaned by the patient or family, and aides clean it only as the care plan says.

Staff do not report to work, or enter a patient's home, with symptoms of a communicable illness such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, an undiagnosed rash or a draining wound, and they call the RN Director. The RN Director decides whether the staff member may work, applying PER-06 and public health guidance.

Reporting of communicable disease: any staff member who finds or suspects a communicable disease or an outbreak in a patient or household, or who is diagnosed with one, reports to the RN Director immediately. The RN Director notifies the patient's practitioner and reports to the local health department or the State Department of Health where the law requires reporting, documenting the date, the person told and the outcome.

The RN Director applies extra precautions when a patient has a communicable disease, tells staff what to wear and what to do, and informs the practitioner and the MLTC plan as needed (see SVC-17). The agency does not refuse care to a patient just because of an infection, including HIV (see CR-06 and SAF-04).

Occupational exposure control: a worker who has a needlestick, cut, splash or other exposure to blood or body fluids immediately washes the area, reports to the RN Director and follows SAF-04. The RN Director records each exposure on the incident log (see SAF-02).

Staff who are required to be screened for TB, vaccinated or masked as set out in PER-06 and PER-07 follow those policies. Personnel records show that screening, immunity and influenza vaccination or mask documentation are on file before direct patient contact.

The RN Director reviews infection data each quarter (infections, exposures, communicable disease reports, hand hygiene observations and supply problems) and reports to the QI committee under GOV-04. The RN Director revises procedures at least annually and after any outbreak or exposure.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the program, writes cleaning and disinfection procedures, trains staff, reports communicable disease and presents infection data to the QI committee.
Assesses infection risk, communicates precautions in the care plan and checks hand hygiene and bag technique at supervisory visits.
Follow Standard Precautions and nursing bag technique and clean equipment between patients.
Follow Standard Precautions, hand hygiene and aide bag technique, use PPE and report illness and exposures.
Provides supplies and resources and makes sure staff health requirements are met.

documentation: Orientation and annual in-service attendance and competency records
Infection risk section of the RN assessment and care plan precautions
Hand hygiene and bag technique observations at supervisory visits and evaluations
Written cleaning and disinfection procedures and equipment cleaning logs
Communicable disease reports and notifications
Exposure reports in the incident log
Quarterly infection data in QI committee minutes

policies.title: HIV and Bloodborne Pathogens Exposure Control
policies.applies_to: All employees, aides, nurses, contractors and volunteers who have direct patient contact or who may be exposed to blood or other potentially infectious material
policies.purpose: To prevent transmission of HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and other bloodborne pathogens in [AGENCY NAME] by requiring barriers and PPE, training at hire and every year, prompt reporting and investigation of every exposure, post-exposure testing, counseling and medical follow-up, confidentiality, and monitoring of the program.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a bloodborne pathogen program that covers barriers, training at hire and yearly, personal protective equipment, monitoring and an exposure-management procedure (10 NYCRR §766.11(l)), and follows 29 CFR 1910.1030. This policy meets Applicant Worksheet p.11 item WS-HIV.1 (HIV/Blood Borne Pathogens policy/procedure: implementation and enforcement for the prevention of HIV or other bloodborne pathogens transmission). The agency applies Universal Precautions to every patient (WS-HIV.2); gives mandatory in-service training at hire and every year (WS-HIV.3); offers post-exposure testing (WS-HIV.4) and post-exposure counseling (WS-HIV.5); keeps HIV information confidential (WS-HIV.6); supplies and requires PPE (WS-HIV.7); names a designated person to whom exposures are reported (WS-HIV.8); provides appropriate medical follow-up for an exposed individual (WS-HIV.9); monitors its prevention program (WS-HIV.10); and investigates every exposure (WS-HIV.11). Each of these is set out in the procedures below. The agency does not discriminate against any patient or employee because of HIV status. Definitions and requirements in State HIV regulations are confirmed by the RN Director against current DOH requirements before each annual review.

definitions.definition: Microorganisms in human blood that can cause disease, including HIV, hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV).
Body fluids such as semen, vaginal secretions, and any body fluid visibly contaminated with blood, and any unfixed tissue or organ.
A specific eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin or parenteral (needlestick, cut or bite) contact with blood or OPIM that results from the performance of an employee's duties.
An approach to infection control in which all human blood and certain body fluids are treated as if known to be infectious for bloodborne pathogens.
The person named by the agency to receive exposure reports, who is the RN Director or, in the RN Director's absence, the on-call RN.
The person whose blood or body fluid was involved in an exposure.

procedures: The Administrator names the RN Director as the Designated Exposure Contact for all exposure reports, and the on-call RN as backup after hours and when the RN Director is unavailable. The name and 24-hour phone number, [PHONE], are posted in the office, given to every employee at orientation, and included on the agency's call directory.

Universal Precautions: all staff treat the blood and body fluids of every patient as infectious, wear PPE as set out in SAF-03, and follow the work practices in this policy. They do not recap, bend, break or reach into containers for sharps, and they never place needles in household trash.

PPE: the agency supplies, at no cost to the employee, gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection, CPR barrier devices and puncture-resistant sharps containers in sizes and quantities needed. Staff wear PPE wherever blood or OPIM contact is expected, remove it before leaving the work area, and dispose of it properly. Staff who lack PPE tell the supervisor at once, and the agency replaces it the same day where possible.

The agency offers hepatitis B vaccination, at no cost, to each employee with possible occupational exposure within 10 working days of starting duty, unless the employee is immune, has already been vaccinated or declines in writing. An employee who declines may change their mind and receive the vaccine later at no cost. (29 CFR 1910.1030.)

Training: the RN Director gives all staff with possible exposure mandatory bloodborne pathogen and HIV training during orientation before patient contact, and again every year in in-service (10 NYCRR §766.11(l); see PER-05). Training covers how bloodborne diseases spread, Universal Precautions, PPE, safe handling of sharps, cleaning of spills, hepatitis B vaccination, what to do after an exposure, confidentiality and non-discrimination. Trainees can ask questions of a qualified person. Attendance is documented in the personnel record.

Spill cleanup: staff put on gloves and other PPE, remove visible material with disposable towels, clean the area with an EPA-registered disinfectant or a fresh 1:10 bleach solution made that day, and dispose of waste as set out in SAF-03.

Immediate action after an exposure: the exposed person immediately washes needlestick, cut or skin contact with soap and water, flushes splashes to the nose or mouth with water, and irrigates eyes with clean water or saline. They do not squeeze the wound or use bleach on the skin.

Reporting: the exposed person reports the exposure at once, within the same shift and as soon as first aid is done, by phone to the Designated Exposure Contact at [PHONE]. Quick reporting matters because post-exposure treatment works best when started within hours. No one is penalized for reporting an exposure.

The Designated Exposure Contact starts the response immediately. The contact sends the employee for medical evaluation and follow-up at [OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH PROVIDER/CLINIC] or the nearest emergency department the same day, within hours of the exposure. The agency pays for evaluation, testing, vaccination, treatment and follow-up at no cost to the employee.

Post-exposure medical follow-up: the health care professional evaluates the exposure and the route, tests the exposed employee's blood with the employee's consent, offers treatment such as post-exposure prophylaxis as medically indicated, offers hepatitis B vaccination or boosters if needed, and sets up counseling and follow-up testing. The agency gives the health care professional a description of the employee's duties, the route of exposure, the source individual's status if known, and relevant vaccination records. The health care professional's written opinion to the agency is limited to whether hepatitis B vaccination is recommended and whether the employee received the evaluation and was told of the results.

Source individual testing: where the source individual is known, the Designated Exposure Contact, with the health care professional, asks for the source's consent to testing, as State law on HIV testing and consent requires, and keeps the results confidential. The agency does not test a patient without lawful consent. If the source declines, the health care professional advises the employee on what to do, and the agency records that the source declined.

Post-exposure counseling: the agency makes counseling available to the exposed employee, at no cost, covering the risk of infection, the meaning of test results, precautions to take while follow-up is under way, symptoms to watch for, and the importance of follow-up testing. Counseling is given by a qualified health professional and can be repeated.

Investigation of every exposure: within 3 business days, the Designated Exposure Contact investigates each exposure to find out what happened, the task, the device or procedure, PPE use, training and whether the exposure could have been prevented. The contact completes an exposure incident report and sends a copy to the Administrator. Any exposure is also recorded under SAF-02.

Corrective action: the RN Director carries out changes found necessary by the investigation, such as additional training, safer devices or supplies, changes to the care plan or work practice, or discipline for willful violations. The RN Director records the action taken and the date.

Confidentiality: HIV-related information and all exposure records are confidential and are kept separately from the personnel file in a locked or access-restricted file. They are disclosed only to the people the law allows, with the employee's or patient's written authorization where required, or as permitted or required by law. Staff who learn a patient's HIV status through their work must not tell anyone who does not need to know for care (see CR-04). Breach of confidentiality leads to discipline.

Non-discrimination: the agency accepts and serves patients regardless of HIV or hepatitis status and does not treat employees differently because of HIV status or because they report an exposure (see CR-06 and PER-10).

Monitoring the program: the RN Director keeps an exposure log without identifying details (date, task, device, PPE, cause, corrective action) and checks compliance through supervisory visit observations, annual evaluations, supply checks and training records. The RN Director reports the data to the QI committee each quarter (see GOV-04).

The RN Director reviews this policy and the exposure control program at least annually and whenever tasks, procedures, devices or laws change, and includes in the review input from the aides and nurses who do the work. The review is documented with the date and the changes made, and the RN Director confirms current requirements in State regulations on HIV and bloodborne pathogens.
Records: employee medical and exposure records are kept as confidential records for the time the law requires (see PER-08 and REC-03), and training records are kept for at least three years.

responsibilities.duty: Receives exposure reports, arranges medical follow-up and counseling, investigates, carries out corrective action, trains staff, monitors the program and reviews the policy annually.
Acts as Designated Exposure Contact after hours and when the RN Director is unavailable.
Pays for vaccination, evaluation, testing and follow-up, provides PPE and supplies, and enforces the policy.
Use Universal Precautions and PPE, report exposures immediately, complete training and keep patient and employee information confidential.
Reviews exposure data and the prevention program each quarter.

documentation: Orientation and annual training attendance records
Hepatitis B vaccination, declination or immunity records (confidential medical file)
Exposure incident report and investigation
Post-exposure evaluation, testing and counseling referral records (confidential)
Health care professional's written opinion
Exposure log and corrective action records
Annual policy review record
QI committee minutes with exposure data
PPE and supply inventory records

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness Plan, Patient Roster and Classification Levels
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] employees, the RN Director, the Administrator, and every patient served in each licensed county
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] can keep care going, or safely and promptly account for every patient, during an emergency. The agency does this by keeping a written emergency plan, an up-to-date patient roster, and a priority ranking of patients by clinical need and transportation need.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a current written Emergency Preparedness Plan and orients all employees to it (10 NYCRR 766.9(c)). The Administrator owns the plan, and the RN Director owns the patient roster and the classification process. The plan is part of the Policy and Procedure Manual that the agency submits to the DOH regional home care office. The regional office must accept the manual before the pre-opening survey (DOH LHCSA Application Requirements FAQ). This policy meets the following items on the Applicant Worksheet: p.9 item WS-EP.1 (Emergency Preparedness Plan addressing the types of emergencies that could impact patient care); p.9 item WS-EP.2 (patient roster); p.10 item WS-EP.13 (procedure to ensure patient contact information is current); p.10 item WS-EP.15 (patient classification levels); and p.10 item WS-EP.16 (Transportation Assistance Levels). SAF-06 covers the communications, call-down, community partner, drill and training items of the plan.

definitions.definition: The written, all-hazards plan describing how the agency will continue or safely modify services and account for patients during an emergency.
A current list of all active patients, kept in a form that can be read if the computer system is down, with the data elements listed in Procedure 6.
The agency's priority ranking of a patient by how urgently services must continue or be checked during an emergency. Level 1 is the highest priority, Level 2 is intermediate, and Level 3 is lowest.

The patient depends on a ventilator or other electricity-dependent equipment for health care needs, or would face immediate risk of serious harm if a visit were missed, for example because there is no informal support and the patient needs hands-on care. Level 1 patients are contacted first.
The patient needs services every day or on most days and has some informal support, but would be at risk if services were interrupted for more than 24 hours.
The patient is stable, has adequate informal support, and can safely have a visit delayed by 72 hours or more, with a telephone check in the meantime.

The agency's rating of the help a patient would need to evacuate. TAL 1: can leave on their own or with family. TAL 2: needs a person's help or a wheelchair-accessible vehicle. TAL 3: needs stretcher, ambulance or other medical transport.
A patient who relies on powered equipment for health care needs, such as a ventilator, oxygen concentrator, suction, hospital bed, or power wheelchair.

procedures: The Administrator writes the Emergency Preparedness Plan before the agency opens. The plan covers at least these emergency types: severe weather (blizzard, ice storm, flooding, coastal storm, extreme heat or cold); loss of electrical power; loss of telephone or computer systems; pandemic or infectious disease outbreak; fire; loss of the agency office or loss of access to it; utility or water failure; transportation shutdown or staff unable to travel; hazardous material release; and civil disturbance or security threat. This addresses Worksheet item WS-EP.1.

For each emergency type, the plan states who is in charge, how patients are prioritized, how staff are notified, how services are continued or modified, and how the agency returns to normal operations.

The Administrator submits the plan with the Policy and Procedure Manual to the DOH regional home care office and corrects any items the regional office identifies. The agency does not begin serving patients until the regional office has accepted the manual and the pre-opening survey is complete.
The Administrator gives every new employee a copy of the plan or its summary at orientation and signs off on completion. In-service is covered in SAF-06.

The Administrator reviews the plan at least once a year and after any drill, real emergency, change of office site, or change of licensed county. The Administrator revises it as needed, records the revision date, and has the RN Director re-train staff (SAF-06).

The RN Director keeps the patient roster. For every active patient it shows: name; home address; patient telephone number; emergency contact telephone number of a family member, caregiver and/or health care proxy (with the name and relationship); Classification Level; Transportation Assistance Level; and whether the patient depends on a ventilator or electricity for health care needs, with the equipment named. This addresses Worksheet item WS-EP.2.

The roster is kept in the agency's secure scheduling/record system. A printed or offline copy is also kept in a secure location and updated at least weekly. The on-call RN can reach it at any hour, and it is protected under CR-04.

At admission, the RN completing the assessment (SVC-05) assigns the patient a Classification Level and a TAL. The RN records both in the clinical record and tells the office staff to enter them on the roster within one business day.

The RN assigns the Classification Level by considering the patient's diagnoses, the hours and tasks of care, medication or treatment needs, availability of informal supports, whether the patient lives alone, and any dependence on electricity or a ventilator. Any patient who depends on a ventilator or electricity for health care needs is Level 1 unless the RN Director documents a reason to rank differently. This addresses Worksheet item WS-EP.15.

The RN assigns the TAL by considering the patient's mobility, cognition, equipment, need for a stretcher or medical transport, and whether family or a vehicle is available. The RN records the TAL on the roster. This addresses Worksheet item WS-EP.16.

The RN reviews and updates the Classification Level and TAL at each reassessment (SVC-05) and whenever a change in condition is reported (SVC-14). The RN notifies office staff the same day so the roster is corrected.

To keep contact information current (Worksheet item WS-EP.13), office staff confirm each patient's address, phone number, emergency contact and health care proxy: (a) at admission; (b) at each RN reassessment; (c) by telephone at least every 90 days; and (d) whenever a weather advisory or other emergency warning is issued, for Level 1 patients first. Aides report any change in contact information to the office within one business day.

Office staff record each verification on the roster with the date and the staff member's initials. If a contact cannot be reached, office staff try the alternate contacts. If none can be reached within 5 business days, they refer it to the RN Director, who decides on a home visit or other follow-up.
Office staff remove discharged patients from the active roster within one business day of the discharge date (SVC-15). They keep the discharge record under REC-02.

At the start of any declared or forecasted emergency, the RN Director pulls the current roster, confirms the Level 1 patients and electricity-dependent patients, and directs the call-down and visit priorities described in SAF-06.
The RN Director gives the Administrator a short summary of roster accuracy (the share of patients verified within the last 90 days) each quarter for review by the QI Committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Writes, reviews and revises the plan; submits it to the regional office; ensures every employee is oriented to it; and ensures the office, equipment and communications support the plan.
Maintains the roster; ensures Classification Levels and TALs are assigned and reviewed; directs patient prioritization during an emergency.
Assigns Classification Level and TAL at admission and reassessment; identifies ventilator and electricity dependence.
Enter and verify roster data on schedule; remove discharged patients; keep the offline roster copy current.
Report changes in patient contact information, condition or equipment to the office within one business day.

documentation: Written Emergency Preparedness Plan with revision dates
Employee orientation sign-off
Current patient roster (electronic and offline copy)
Assessment record showing Classification Level and TAL
Contact verification log (date, method, initials)
Quarterly roster accuracy summary to QI Committee
Regional office acceptance of the Policy and Procedure Manual

policies.title: Emergency Communications, Call-Down, Community Partners, Drills and Staff Training
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN Director, office staff, nurses, personal care aides and all other employees
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] can reach its staff, patients, the Department of Health and community emergency agencies during an emergency, and that staff know and practice what to do.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains the communication tools, partner contacts, drills and training that put its written emergency plan into practice (10 NYCRR 766.9(c)). The agency also keeps its Health Commerce System (HCS) accounts and 24-hour emergency contacts current (10 NYCRR 766.9(o); see GOV-07). This policy meets the following Applicant Worksheet items: p.9 item WS-EP.3 (call-down list of current staff and how it is kept current); p.9 item WS-EP.4 (communications if telephone/computer network become unavailable); pp.9-10 item WS-EP.5 (contact list of community partners: local health department, local emergency management, emergency medical services, local law enforcement); p.10 item WS-EP.6 (response to requests for information by community partners); p.10 item WS-EP.7 (participation in agency-specific or community-wide drills and exercises); p.10 item WS-EP.8 (what staff do when a patient refuses mandatory evacuation); p.10 item WS-EP.9 (communications with the DOH through the HCS); p.10 item WS-EP.10 (responding to home care emergency response surveys); p.10 item WS-EP.11 (in-service of staff at orientation, yearly and with any revisions); p.10 item WS-EP.12 (emergency response drills); and p.10 item WS-EP.14 (alternate communications if telephones/internet are unavailable).

definitions.definition: A current list of all employees with phone numbers and alternates, arranged so that each person calls a set of others, starting with the Administrator and RN Director.
The local health department, local emergency management office, emergency medical services, and local law enforcement for each county the agency is licensed to serve.
An evacuation order issued by a government authority for the area where a patient lives.
A request from the Department of Health, sent through the HCS, for the agency to report its operating status, patient impact or needs during an emergency.
The NYS Department of Health Health Commerce System, the secure portal through which DOH communicates with the agency and the agency reports to DOH.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a staff call-down list showing each employee's name, role, home and mobile numbers, personal email, and an alternate contact. The list also has the 24/7 emergency contacts the agency has given DOH. This addresses Worksheet item WS-EP.3.

The Administrator updates the call-down list within 2 business days of any hire, separation, change of phone number, or change of job. Office staff verify every entry with the employee at least every quarter. The Administrator keeps a printed copy off-site and with the on-call RN.

In an emergency, the Administrator or RN Director starts the call-down. Each caller reaches the people assigned to them, records the time reached, and reports back to the person who called. If someone cannot be reached after two attempts, the caller notes it and reports it to the RN Director.

Alternate communications (Worksheet items WS-EP.4 and WS-EP.14): the plan lists backup methods if telephones or the internet are down. These are mobile phones on separate carriers, text messaging, personal email, a backup mobile hotspot, and the printed roster and call-down list. If all electronic methods fail, supervisors go in person to the homes of Level 1 patients and electricity-dependent patients, and aides on shift report in person to the nearest agency or supervisor location. The Administrator tests the alternate methods at least once a year.

The Administrator keeps a contact list of community partners (Worksheet item WS-EP.5). It names, for each county in the license, the local health department, local emergency management office, emergency medical services, and local law enforcement, with 24-hour numbers and email. The Administrator verifies the list at least every six months and after any licensed county is added.

Responding to community partner requests (Worksheet item WS-EP.6): the Administrator or the RN Director on duty is the single point of contact. They give the information requested, such as the numbers and locations of Level 1 and electricity-dependent patients, or the agency's operating status, only as the Privacy Policy (CR-04) allows for emergency situations. They log each request and what was sent, with the date, time and person who received it.

Communications with DOH through the HCS (Worksheet item WS-EP.9): the Administrator ensures that at least two employees hold active HCS accounts with the correct roles, and that the HCS communication directory and 24/7 emergency contacts are updated at least monthly (GOV-07). During an emergency, the Administrator checks the HCS at least twice a day and posts or acts on every DOH communication.

The Administrator submits the weekly HERDS report, which includes patient census by licensed county, in the HCS window that opens Tuesday at 8:00 a.m. and closes Thursday at 2:00 p.m. (DOH DAL DHCBS 25-09). The Administrator keeps a copy of each submission. If the report cannot be submitted, the Administrator contacts hcstatrpts@health.ny.gov before the window closes.

Home care emergency response surveys (Worksheet item WS-EP.10): when a survey arrives through the HCS, the Administrator or the RN Director completes it promptly and within the time DOH sets. They get patient counts and status from the current roster (SAF-05), keep a copy of the response, and note the date and time submitted.

Drills and exercises (Worksheet items WS-EP.7 and WS-EP.12): the Administrator schedules and runs at least one agency-specific emergency response drill each year. It tests the call-down, the alternate communications, and the use of the roster to prioritize patients. The agency also takes part in community-wide exercises that its local health department or emergency management office invites it to join. The Administrator records the date, scenario, participants, time taken to reach staff, and findings in a written drill report, and the QI Committee reviews it (GOV-04).
After each drill or real emergency, the Administrator and RN Director hold a debrief within 14 days, list corrective actions with a responsible person and due date, and revise the plan if needed.

Patient refusing mandatory evacuation (Worksheet item WS-EP.8): staff do not use force or put themselves at risk. The employee (a) tells the patient clearly about the order and the danger; (b) offers help to reach transportation and contacts the patient's family or health care proxy; (c) if the patient still refuses and has decision-making capacity, respects the choice and does not argue; (d) if the patient lacks capacity, or seems at imminent risk, calls the RN Director and, if needed, 911; (e) leaves the area when staff safety requires it; and (f) records the refusal in the clinical record.

After any refusal, the RN Director informs the patient's emergency contact or health care proxy, informs the local emergency management office as CR-04 allows, flags the patient on the roster for follow-up by phone as soon as it is safe, and keeps a note of every contact attempt.

Training (Worksheet item WS-EP.11): the RN Director or Administrator trains every new employee on the emergency plan at orientation, before they are assigned to patients. Every employee is trained again at least once a year. Everyone is also trained again, within 30 days, after any revision of the plan. Training covers the call-down, roster priorities, alternate communications, safety in the home, and the evacuation refusal steps.

The trainer records each session with the date, topics, trainer, attendees' signatures and a short check of understanding. The RN Director follows up with anyone who misses training within 14 days. Records are kept in the personnel file (PER-08).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the call-down list, partner contacts and HCS accounts; submits the weekly HERDS report; responds to DOH surveys; runs drills; ensures training occurs.
Leads patient prioritization and welfare checks; handles evacuation refusals; trains clinical staff; serves as backup point of contact for community partners.
Verify call-down entries; log partner requests; keep the printed roster and contact lists current.
Keep their contact details current; answer the call-down; follow the plan; report problems or patient refusals to the RN Director.

documentation: Call-down list with update dates and quarterly verification record
Alternate communications test record
Community partner contact list with verification dates
Log of community partner information requests
HCS account list and HERDS submission copies
Copies of DOH emergency response survey responses
Drill reports, debriefs and corrective action logs
Evacuation refusal notes in the clinical record
Emergency plan training attendance records

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All employees who work in patients' homes or at the agency office, and their supervisors
policies.purpose: To protect employees from hazards in patients' homes and at the agency, including violence, unsafe lifting and unsafe home conditions, and to make clear that employees may leave an unsafe situation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a workplace free of recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious physical harm, in line with the OSHA General Duty Clause (29 USC 654). The RN checks the home environment at assessment and reports unsafe conditions, as part of the clinical supervision the agency provides (10 NYCRR 766.5(b)). Employees may leave any unsafe situation and must report it to the RN Director. The agency trains employees in violence prevention, ergonomics, and safe lifting and transfers, as part of orientation and in-service (10 NYCRR 766.11(i)). Bloodborne pathogen safety is covered in SAF-04, and infection control in SAF-03. No employee is disciplined for leaving a situation they reasonably believe is unsafe.

definitions.definition: Any threat or act of physical violence, harassment, intimidation or other threatening behavior directed at an employee by a patient, family member, visitor, co-worker or other person, in a patient's home, at the agency office or while traveling for work.

A condition in which the employee reasonably believes they face a risk of harm. Examples: threats or violence, weapons, intoxicated or aggressive persons, unsafe animals, fire or gas hazards, serious infestation, structural hazards, or a task that cannot be done safely.
Lifting, transferring and repositioning done according to the plan of care, using proper body mechanics and equipment, with return demonstration of the technique.

procedures: Before the first visit, the RN reviews the referral for known risks (history of violence, weapons, pets, neighborhood hazards, lack of utilities) and records them in the clinical record. The RN Director tells the assigned aide before the first visit.

At the assessment (SVC-05), the RN evaluates the home environment: access and lighting, stairs, clutter, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, electrical and heating hazards, pests, pets, firearms, smoking, oxygen use, and available equipment. The RN records hazards and any actions agreed to, and reports unsafe conditions to the RN Director within one business day.

If the home cannot be made safe enough for staff to work in, the RN Director discusses changes with the patient and family, asks the MLTC plan or referral source for help if needed (SVC-17), and documents each step. If the hazard remains, the RN Director follows the discharge process in SVC-15.

At orientation (PER-05), and again at least annually, every employee who works in homes is trained in: violence and aggression prevention and de-escalation; recognizing warning signs; ergonomics; safe lifting, transfers and repositioning with return demonstration; fire and electrical safety; personal safety when traveling and entering homes; and how to report. Training is recorded in the personnel record.

Every employee carries agency photo identification, showing name, title and agency name, at all times while working and shows it on request. The employee returns the identification when employment ends.

The aide follows the Aide Care Plan and does not do transfers or lifts that the plan does not call for, that the aide has not been trained to do, or that need equipment or a second person who is not available. The aide calls the RN Director for guidance before doing the task.

If an employee feels unsafe, the employee may leave. The employee moves to a safe place, calls 911 if there is danger, and then calls the RN Director or on-call supervisor as soon as possible, and in any case the same day. The employee is not required to stay or to finish the shift.
