The Administrator refers serious violations for reporting to the appropriate authority, including the licensing board, law enforcement or other agencies, as SAF-01 and the law require.
Boundary and conduct standards are reviewed in annual in-service training and in the annual performance evaluation, including the in-home observation visit where applicable. See PER-01 and PER-05.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually with the personnel policies required under 10 NYCRR 766.11.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the policy, decides discipline, and refers serious violations for reporting.
Teaches the policy, investigates reports involving clients, and observes conduct during supervisory visits.
Coach staff on boundaries, receive reports of gifts and boundary concerns, and escalate quickly.
Collects signed acknowledgments and keeps discipline and investigation records.
Follow this policy, report concerns, and never accept gifts or financial involvement.

documentation: Signed policy acknowledgments in personnel files
Orientation and in-service attendance records
Gift or boundary incident reports
Investigation files and discipline records
Performance evaluations covering conduct

policies.title: Patient Care Clinical Record
policies.applies_to: All patients of [AGENCY NAME] and all staff who create, use, store, remove or release patient information.
policies.purpose: To make sure every patient has a complete, accurate and confidential clinical record that documents the care given, and that records are protected against loss and unauthorized access.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a confidential clinical record for each patient, as required by 10 NYCRR 766.6(a). This policy meets Applicant Worksheet p.7 items WS-CR.1 through WS-CR.16. WS-CR.1 (Patient Care Clinical Record policy/procedure, referencing HIPAA): this policy is written to operate with the agency's privacy policy CR-04 and the HIPAA administrative requirements in 45 CFR 164.530. WS-CR.2 (confidentiality): all patient records and information are confidential and are shared only as the patient authorizes or the law allows. WS-CR.3 (safeguards against loss or unauthorized use): records are kept in locked storage or in a password-protected system with role-based access, audit logging and backup, as required by 10 NYCRR 766.6(e). WS-CR.4 (use, removal and release of information): use, removal and release are governed by the procedures below. The record contains: WS-CR.5 identifying patient data; WS-CR.6 medical orders; WS-CR.7 nursing assessments; WS-CR.8 the plan of care; WS-CR.9 signed and dated progress notes for each visit or phone contact by professional staff; WS-CR.10 RN supervisory reports; WS-CR.11 observations and reports made by aides to RNs, LPNs or therapists; WS-CR.12 aide activity sheets; WS-CR.13 documentation of accidents and incidents; WS-CR.14 documentation of the patient's receipt of the Bill of Rights, as required by 10 NYCRR 766.1(a)(1); and WS-CR.15 discharge planning and a discharge summary. WS-CR.16: the agency notifies the authorized practitioner of changes in the patient's condition and documents the notification in the record. Electronic records are secure, confidential and printable on request, as required by 10 NYCRR 766.12(b). Records are available to DOH.

definitions.definition: The confidential file, paper or electronic, holding all documentation of a patient's care and services.
The physician, nurse practitioner or other licensed practitioner who is legally authorized to order the patient's care.
A signed and dated entry by professional staff after each visit or phone contact describing what was done, observed and reported.
The record in which an aide documents the tasks done and observations made at each visit.
Any disclosure of record content to a person or organization outside the agency.

procedures: At admission, the intake coordinator opens a clinical record in the agency's records system and enters identifying data (WS-CR.5): name, address, date of birth, contact and emergency contacts, payer, representative if any, and the authorized practitioner.

Before care starts, staff give the patient the Bill of Rights and obtain a signed or documented acknowledgment. The acknowledgment is filed in the record, or the reason it could not be signed is documented (WS-CR.14, 766.1(a)(1)).
The RN files each medical order, including verbal orders that the RN has documented and sent for signature, in the record when received (WS-CR.6). See SVC-07.
The RN files the initial assessment and each reassessment in the record (WS-CR.7) and the plan of care and each update (WS-CR.8). See SVC-05 and SVC-06.
Each RN, LPN or therapist signs and dates a progress note after each visit or phone contact with or about the patient (WS-CR.9) and files it in the record within [TIMEFRAME, e.g., 24 hours].
The RN files each supervisory report in the record (WS-CR.10). See SVC-09 and SVC-10.

Aides document the tasks done and their observations on the activity sheet at every visit (WS-CR.12). Aides report observations and changes to the RN, LPN or therapist as soon as noticed, and the RN documents the report and any action in a note (WS-CR.11). See SVC-08.

When a patient's condition changes, the RN notifies the authorized practitioner promptly, documents the date, time, person notified, information given and orders received, and files this in the record (WS-CR.16). See SVC-14.
Any accident or incident involving a patient is documented in an incident report and a note in the record (WS-CR.13). See SAF-02.
At discharge, the RN documents discharge planning and completes a discharge summary that is signed, dated and filed (WS-CR.15). See SVC-15.

Records are kept in locked cabinets in a locked office, or in electronic systems that require unique user logins, limit access by role, log access and are backed up. Staff may view only the records needed for their job (WS-CR.2, WS-CR.3).

Records may not be removed from the agency office except by licensed or authorized staff who need them for care, and only the minimum needed. The staff member signs out the record and returns it by [TIMEFRAME]. Paper in a client's home or in staff vehicles is kept secured and out of view.
Staff use only agency-approved devices and systems. They do not text, email or post patient information on personal or unsecured channels.

Release of information (WS-CR.4): the Privacy Officer releases records only with the patient's or representative's written authorization or as the law permits, such as to DOH, to treating providers for care, or to payers for payment. Each release is logged with date, recipient, content, purpose and who released it. See CR-04.
Patients or representatives may request to see or obtain copies of their records. The Privacy Officer verifies identity and responds under the agency's privacy procedures.
On request, electronic records are printed or exported in readable form and made available to DOH (766.12(b)).
Late or corrected entries are marked as such, dated and signed. Original entries are never deleted or obscured.
The RN Director reviews a sample of records each quarter for completeness and timeliness and reports the results to the QI Committee. See GOV-04.
Staff who lose a record, send information to the wrong person, or access records without need report it to the Privacy Officer the same day, and the agency responds under CR-04.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and ensures records are safeguarded.
Ensures secure storage and systems are in place, and enforces discipline for record violations.
Ensures records are complete, timely and accurate, and audits them quarterly.
Controls access and release, keeps the disclosure log and handles breaches under CR-04.
Create and file required documents, sign and date entries, and notify practitioners of changes.
Complete activity sheets at each visit and report observations to the RN, LPN or therapist.

documentation: Clinical record for each patient with all contents listed in this policy
Signed Bill of Rights acknowledgment
Release of information log and authorizations
Record sign-out log
Electronic system access logs and backup records
Quarterly record audit results

policies.title: Client Records Retention and Agency Closure
policies.applies_to: All patient clinical records of [AGENCY NAME], in paper or electronic form, and the Governing Authority and Administrator responsible for them if the agency closes.
policies.purpose: To make sure patient records are kept for the required period, are available after discharge, and are protected and accessible even if the agency stops operating.
policies.policy: This policy meets Applicant Worksheet p.7 items WS-CR.17 through WS-CR.20. WS-CR.17: [AGENCY NAME] keeps each patient record for at least 6 years after discharge, as required by 10 NYCRR 766.6(b). WS-CR.18: for a patient who is a minor, the record is kept until 6 years after discharge or 3 years after the patient reaches age 18, whichever is longer (766.6(c)). WS-CR.19: if the agency discontinues operation, the governing authority arranges for the records to be maintained, stored and accessible (766.6(d)). WS-CR.20: the governing authority informs DOH in writing where the records are kept (766.6(d)). Records are kept securely throughout the retention period and are available to DOH. Electronic records remain secure, confidential and printable on request (766.12(b)). Records are not destroyed before the end of the retention period, or while a legal hold, audit, investigation or open complaint applies. HIPAA documentation required by 45 CFR 164.530(j) is kept for the period that rule requires.

definitions.definition: The minimum time a record must be kept: 6 years after discharge, or for a minor, 6 years after discharge or 3 years after age 18, whichever is longer.
The date the agency's services to the patient end, as documented in the discharge summary.
A directive that stops destruction of records because of an investigation, audit, lawsuit or complaint.
The person or entity that holds the records and gives access after the agency closes.

procedures: At discharge, the Medical Records Coordinator records the discharge date and calculates the earliest destruction date for the record. For an adult it is 6 years after discharge. For a minor it is the later of 6 years after discharge or 3 years after the patient's 18th birthday. The date goes in the retention schedule.

After discharge, the Medical Records Coordinator closes the record, confirms the discharge summary is filed, and moves the record to secure archive storage in locked storage or an access-controlled electronic archive.
Archived records stay indexed by patient name and discharge date so they can be found quickly for patients, authorized requesters and DOH.
Electronic archives are backed up on a schedule set by [IT/RECORDS VENDOR]. The Administrator tests restoration at least annually to confirm records are readable and printable.

Each year, the Medical Records Coordinator lists records that have passed their retention period. The Administrator confirms there is no legal hold, audit, investigation or open complaint before approving destruction in writing.

Approved records are destroyed by shredding or secure electronic deletion so they cannot be read or rebuilt. A destruction log shows the date, method, who destroyed them, and the record identifiers. Where a vendor is used, there is a signed agreement protecting confidentiality.

The Administrator places a legal hold when notified of a DOH review, lawsuit, billing audit, or complaint, and no hold-affected record is destroyed until the Administrator releases the hold in writing.
Release of archived records follows REC-01 and CR-04. Requests are logged, and identity and authority are verified.

If the governing authority decides to close the agency, it notifies the Administrator and begins a written records closure plan before the closing date. This is coordinated with GOV-08 where ownership is changing.

The closure plan names the records custodian, which may be a storage company, a successor agency, or another responsible entity under written agreement. It sets the storage location, security measures, how patients, practitioners and DOH can reach records, and who pays for storage through the retention period.
The records custodian agreement requires confidentiality, secure storage, retention for the full required period, a way to find records by patient, and prompt access on request.
The governing authority notifies DOH in writing of where the records are kept, including the custodian's name, address, phone and a contact person, and updates DOH if the location changes.
Before closing, the Administrator transfers or arranges continued care for active patients under SVC-15. The Administrator transfers each record to the custodian and keeps a transfer inventory.
The Administrator keeps a copy of the closure plan, DOH notification and the transfer inventory with the agency's permanent governance records, and gives the plan to the new custodian.
The Administrator reviews this policy and the retention schedule at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Arranges for storage and access of records if the agency closes and notifies DOH in writing of their location.
Approves destruction, places legal holds, tests archive restoration and carries out the closure plan.
Calculates retention dates, archives records, maintains the destruction log and indexes.
Controls release of archived records and protects confidentiality.
Stores records securely and provides access after closure as agreed in writing.

documentation: Retention schedule with discharge dates and earliest destruction dates
Destruction approvals and destruction log
Legal hold notices and releases
Archive backup and restoration test records
Records closure plan, custodian agreement and transfer inventory
Written notice to DOH of records location

policies.title: Agency Records and Reports Retention
policies.applies_to: The Governing Authority, Administrator and all staff who create or keep agency administrative, governance, financial and personnel records at the principal office and any branch office.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps the required agency records and reports for the required time, in the right location, secure, and ready for DOH.
policies.policy: This policy meets Applicant Worksheet p.12 items WS-REC.1 through WS-REC.4. WS-REC.1 (Records and Reports policy: retention time frames, where records are kept, and what is kept): records and reports are kept for the time frames in this policy at the principal office, in the location set out below. WS-REC.2: the principal office in New York State keeps the license issued by the Department; the certificate of incorporation or articles (if applicable); the partnership agreement (if applicable); the certificate of doing business under an assumed name (if applicable); contracts and agreements related to patient care; the rules and bylaws of the governing authority and QA bylaws; operating policies and procedures; a current patient roster; and a listing of all personnel (10 NYCRR 766.12(a)(1)). Any branch office keeps the policies, a personnel list and patient records (766.12(a)(2)). WS-REC.3: the agency keeps and makes available to DOH on request the governing authority meeting minutes and committee meeting minutes (3 years); records of all financial transactions related to patient care (3 years); personnel records (3 years after separation); patient clinical records (per REC-01 and REC-02, at least 6 years after discharge); and grievance and complaint records (3 years after resolution). All records are held in hard copy or electronic form and are secured. WS-REC.4: each year the agency provides DOH with statistical summaries and, if applicable, the list of stockholders and shareholders, the list of directors, officers and corporate members, and any documents related to the Securities and Exchange Commission (766.12(c)). Wage parity records are kept longer, for 10 years, as stated in PER-09. The agency also promptly submits all other records and reports DOH requires (766.12(a)); see REC-04.

definitions.definition: The agency's main office in New York State, which holds the records listed in 766.12(a)(1).
An agency office other than the principal office, which keeps policies, a personnel list and patient records.
The current list of patients served, kept up to date and used for emergency planning under SAF-05.
The minimum length of time a record must be kept before it can be destroyed.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a Records Retention Schedule that lists each record type, who is responsible, where it is kept, its format, and the retention period. The Governing Authority approves it, and it is reviewed at least annually.

The Administrator keeps the following at the principal office: the license, certificate of incorporation or articles, partnership agreement, assumed-name certificate (as applicable), patient-care contracts, governing-authority and QA bylaws, current policies and procedures, the current patient roster and the personnel list (WS-REC.2).

The Medical Records Coordinator updates the patient roster whenever patients are admitted or discharged, and at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., weekly]. HR updates the personnel list when staff are hired or leave.
At any branch office, the branch manager keeps the current policies, personnel list and patient records and confirms this at least annually.

The Governing Authority secretary keeps governing authority meeting minutes, and each committee chair keeps committee minutes, including the QI Committee. They are signed, dated and filed within [TIMEFRAME] of each meeting and kept at least 3 years.
The Finance Manager keeps records of all financial transactions related to patient care, including billing, claims, payments, remittances and refunds, for at least 3 years.
Human Resources keeps personnel records for at least 3 years after the employee's separation (see PER-08). Health records are kept separate and confidential.
The Administrator keeps the complaint log and all complaint and grievance records for at least 3 years after resolution (see CR-03).
Patient clinical records are retained as stated in REC-01 and REC-02, at least 6 years after discharge, and longer for minors.
Paper records are kept in locked storage with limited access. Electronic records are kept in secure systems with logins, role-based access and backup, are confidential, and can be printed on request.

Records are never destroyed before their retention period ends. Before any destruction the Administrator approves in writing and confirms no legal hold, audit, investigation or open complaint applies. Destruction is by shredding or secure deletion and is logged.
If DOH asks to see records, the Administrator or designee provides them promptly, in the form requested, and logs what was provided and when.

Each year the Administrator prepares the statistical summaries of services and reimbursement and the ownership information that DOH requires, and submits them by the DOH deadline. The ownership information includes stockholders and shareholders, directors, officers and corporate members, and any SEC documents, if applicable (WS-REC.4).
The Administrator confirms the annual reports are filed and keeps a copy of each submission and proof of filing with the records.
Wage parity records are kept for 10 years under PER-09, so the Administrator ensures the Retention Schedule shows 10 years for those records.
The Administrator reviews this policy and the Records Retention Schedule at least annually and updates them for any change in law.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the Records Retention Schedule, keeps its own minutes, and ensures required records are kept.
Keeps principal office records, approves destruction, responds to DOH requests and files annual reports.
Keeps patient-care financial records and supplies data for annual statistical summaries.
Keeps personnel records and the personnel list.
Keeps the patient roster and manages clinical record retention.
Keep the policies, personnel list and patient records required at the branch.

documentation: Records Retention Schedule
Principal office records binder or index showing each required document
Meeting minutes of governing authority and committees
Financial transaction records for patient care
Complaint and grievance log and files
Destruction approvals and log
Copies of annual statistical and ownership submissions with proof of filing

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: The Administrator and all staff responsible for preparing, reviewing or filing reports and registrations required by NYS DOH and related agencies.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] submits every record and report the Department of Health requires, accurately and on time, and keeps its license and payment status in good standing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will ensure prompt submission of all records and reports required by the DOH. This policy meets Applicant Worksheet p.8 item WS-GA.6. The agency submits all records and reports DOH requires (10 NYCRR 766.12(a)). This includes weekly HERDS reporting of patient census by licensed county, with the reporting window opening Tuesday at 8:00 a.m. and closing Thursday at 2:00 p.m. (DAL DHCBS 25-09). It includes annual LHCSA registration under Public Health Law §3605-b. An unregistered agency may not operate or be paid, a late registration carries a penalty of $500 per month, and missing two registration periods can lead to revocation. It includes cost reports when DOH requires them under Public Health Law §3612, filed within 90 days of notice, with a 30-day correction window. It includes the annual statistical summaries and ownership list under 10 NYCRR 766.12(c). If the agency performs Medicaid work in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk or Westchester, it files the annual wage parity certification and independently audited statement required by Public Health Law §3614-c. The Administrator is accountable for all filings and keeps a reporting calendar.

definitions.definition: The Health Emergency Response Data System, through which LHCSAs report weekly census by licensed county.
The yearly LHCSA registration required by Public Health Law §3605-b.
A financial report on agency costs that DOH requires under Public Health Law §3612 when it issues notice.
The annual certification, with an independently audited statement, that the agency met wage parity for covered Medicaid work.
The agency's schedule listing each required report, its deadline, the responsible person and the filing status.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a Reporting Calendar listing each recurring and one-time report or registration, its deadline, who prepares it, who reviews it and who submits it. A backup person is named for each item.
The Administrator makes sure the staff who file reports have active Health Commerce System accounts, as set out in GOV-07, and that the agency's contact directory is current.

Weekly HERDS: [HERDS COORDINATOR] compiles the patient census by licensed county from the current patient roster, no later than Tuesday morning, and enters it in HERDS after the window opens at 8:00 a.m. Tuesday.

The Administrator or designee checks the HERDS submission each week and confirms it was completed before the window closes Thursday at 2:00 p.m. A confirmation is saved. If the system cannot be accessed, the coordinator contacts hcstatrpts@health.ny.gov before the window closes.

If a HERDS submission is missed or found wrong, the coordinator corrects or submits it as soon as possible, tells the Administrator, documents the cause and fixes it. Backup coverage is used during planned absences.

Annual registration: the Administrator completes and submits the LHCSA annual registration under PHL §3605-b by the DOH deadline, confirms receipt, and files the confirmation. The agency does not provide or bill for services in any period when it is not registered.

The Administrator sets a reminder at least 60 days before the registration deadline and rechecks status 30 days before. Missed registrations are treated as an urgent compliance problem, with the late penalty of $500 per month and possible revocation after two missed periods.

Cost reports: when DOH notifies the agency that a cost report is required, the Administrator logs the notice date and sets the due date within 90 days. The Finance Manager prepares the report, the Administrator and an outside accountant review it, and it is filed on time.
If DOH requests corrections to a cost report, the Finance Manager provides the corrected information within the 30-day correction window.

Annual statistical and ownership reports: each year the Administrator prepares the statistical summaries of services and reimbursement and the ownership list under 766.12(c), including stockholders, directors, officers and SEC documents where applicable, and files them by the DOH deadline. See REC-03.

Wage parity: if the agency provides Medicaid home care in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk or Westchester, the Finance Manager and Administrator complete the annual certification and arrange the independently audited statement under PER-09. They file them as required and keep the records for 10 years.

Other DOH requests: when DOH requests records or reports, the Administrator logs the request, sets the deadline, assigns a responsible person, provides the materials promptly and keeps a copy and proof of submission.
Every filing is reviewed for accuracy by someone other than the preparer before submission. The Administrator keeps copies and confirmations in the reporting file.
The Administrator reviews the Reporting Calendar monthly and reports any late or missed filings and corrective actions to the Governing Authority and the QI Committee under GOV-04.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually and updates it when DOH changes a report, deadline or system.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures resources and oversight so required reports are filed, and reviews reports of late or missed filings.
Owns the Reporting Calendar, files registration and annual reports, and ensures corrections are made.
Compiles and submits weekly HERDS census within the Tuesday 8:00 a.m. to Thursday 2:00 p.m. window.
Prepares cost reports, financial statistics and wage parity documents.
Keeps the patient roster and county data accurate for census reporting.
Files assigned reports when the primary person is unavailable.

Cost report notices, submissions and correction records

Wage parity certification and audited statement, kept 10 years

Records of late or missed filings and corrective actions

documents.title: LHCSA Applicant Worksheet
documents.form_number: None printed on the form (Division of Home and Community Based Services, 'FINAL: December 2016')
documents.issuer: NYS Department of Health, Division of Home and Community Based Services
documents.version: FINAL: December 2016. This is the version posted on the DOH 'Guidance Documents for LHCSA Applicants' page. I did not find a newer one.
documents.how_used: Primary checklist (doc 0). DOH says applicants 'should use this form as a guide to assess the completeness of the Policy and Procedure Manual', and that it 'must be submitted with the Policy and Procedure Manual'. A policy must be submitted for each service requested. The form has no item numbers, so the item_ids below are positional: a section code plus the order of the bullets in the document. Only sections that apply to a personal-care LHCSA are listed. Nursing is included because Review Tool Part A marks it as required for every LHCSA. Personal Care Aide is included. The Home Health Aide, therapy, social work, nutrition, homemaker, housekeeper, physician and medical-supply sections apply only if the agency is approved for those services, so I left them out.

documents.title: NYSDOH LHCSA P & P Review Tool PART A (Initial Review Tool)
documents.issuer: NYS Department of Health, Division of Home and Community Based Services
documents.how_used: Doc 1. This is the DOH initial-review checklist. It sets the minimum list of policies, the per-policy format elements, the per-service job description and P&P requirement, and the program materials that must come with the manual. Items are numbered A-1, A-2, and so on, in the document's order. The document itself has no numbering.

documents.title: NYSDOH LHCSA P & P Manual Review Tool PART B (regulation crosswalk)
documents.issuer: NYS Department of Health, Division of Home and Community Based Services
documents.how_used: Doc 2. The regional-office surveyor uses this tool. It copies the text of 10 NYCRR Parts 765, 766, 402 and 403 and grades each policy's statement, procedure and overall acceptability. The item_ids use the document's own regulation numbering. Only provisions that require written policies, procedures or plans, or that the agency must address in its policies, are listed. Text is condensed with '…'.

documents.title: Guidance for Developing Policies and Procedures for a Licensed Home Care Services Agency (LHCSA)
documents.issuer: NYS Department of Health, Office of Primary Care and Health Systems Management, Division of Home and Community Based Services
documents.how_used: Doc 3. This sets the submission rules and the required format of each policy. Those are summarised in 'notes' and in the G items. Attachment B is the sample index with a regulatory crosswalk. Attachment C lists the materials due before the pre-opening survey.

required_items.text: Patient Rights policy/procedure – refers to: written and verbal notification of the patient's rights
documentation of providing patient rights
Advising or informing the patient of: the services the agency provides
the cost of the services
their responsibility for payment after insurance (third party payers)
any changes to services in 30 calendar days from the date of change
services, and when and how services are to be provided
the right to participate in planning their care
the name, title and functions of who will provide services
any changes to their plan of care
Patient's right to: refuse care and treatment
voice complaints and grievances
contact the NYS Department of Health to voice complaints and grievances
be treated with consideration, respect and dignity
privacy, including confidential treatment of his/her patient records
refuse the release of their records to any outside agency
have a legal representative if the patient lacks capacity
The policy provides the: procedure to voice complaints and grievances
NYS Department of Health complaint hotline number
Nursing policy/procedure (required service) – includes: Responsibilities of nursing staff consistent with Nursing Practice standards
the need for physician's orders
who will provide the nursing services
References: scope of practice
standards of practice
assessments (initial, reassessment)
patient/caregiver education
medications and treatments
supervision of aides
coordination of services
clinical conferencing
clinical documentation
the plan of care
discharge planning
Personal Care Aide (PCA) policy/procedure – references: the duties and responsibilities of the PCA
scope of task
the need for a physician's order
who will supervise the PCA including frequency
orientation to the care plan
the aide care plan
communication process for changes in patient condition
documentation of tasks
6 hours of in-service training yearly
Admissions policy/procedure – references: admission criteria
that patients are accepted without discrimination
patient acceptance is based on the agency's ability to provide care consistent with patient's assessed needs
patient needs can be met safely and adequately by the agency
the notification/explanation of costs, insurance, and expectation of payment
written notification of patient rights
informed consent
Discharge Planning policy/procedure – references the: need to initiate discharge planning prior to discharge
need for a safe, timely and appropriate discharge or transfer
notification to the authorized practitioner at least 48 hours prior to discharge
consultation with the patient/caregiver of the discharge plan
consultation with other professional staff of the discharge plan
Plan of Care policy/procedure – the plan of care is: based on the RN initial assessment
established for each patient
based on assessed identified patient's needs
reviewed and revised as frequently as necessary to reflect changes in patient condition
needed to be reviewed and revised at least every 6 months
needed to be documented in the clinical record
The plan of care must include: a pertinent diagnosis and prognosis
any identified need for palliative care
the patient's mental/emotional status
the frequency of each service to be provided
medications
treatments
diet regimens
functional limitations and rehabilitation potential
orders for therapy services including specific procedures and modalities if needed
the frequency and duration of all services ordered
Medical Orders policy/procedure – states: an order from the patient's authorized practitioner will be obtained for all patients
who is an authorized practitioner (medical doctor, doctor of Osteopathy, doctor of Podiatry, licensed midwife or nurse practitioner)
orders are to be reviewed and revised as the needs of the patient change
the orders will be reviewed and revised at a minimum every 6 months
all orders are to reference all diagnoses, medications, treatments, prognoses, need for palliative care, any other pertinent information relevant to the patient's plan of care
all orders are to be authenticated by the authorized practitioner within 12 months
changes in medical orders, including telephone orders, are to be authenticated by the authorized practitioner within 12 months
References: how orders will be obtained
discharge planning
verbal orders
Clinical Supervision policy/procedure – references: the supervision of all services
the supervision of paraprofessional staff
that the agency shall employ sufficient numbers of supervisory staff to ensure quality patient care services are provided
that staff are routinely supervised to ensure care is provided according to the plan of care
that supervision will include in-home visits and the frequency of supervisory visits
that all staff will be assigned according to their licensure, discipline, training, orientation and demonstrated skills
that plans of care must be revised as needed
clinical consultation, orientation, and training for staff
RN Supervision policy/procedure – states that: the RN supervisor will conduct in-home visits on the initial aide service visit
the supervisor will demonstrate to and instruct the aide in the treatments/services to be provided
the RN supervisor will conduct in-home visits minimally every 6 months
the RN supervisor will conduct in-home visits for a change in patient condition, needs or environment
the supervisor will instruct and review written reports
all supervision will be recorded in writing
Patient Care Clinical Record policy/procedure – references: HIPPA [sic]
confidentiality
Safeguards against loss or unauthorized use
use, removal and release of information
Part of the patient care record: identifying patient data
medical orders
nursing assessments
plan of care
signed/dated progress notes for each visit or phone contact by professional staff
supervisory reports
observations and reports made to RNs, LPNs, or therapists
aide activity sheets
documentation of accidents/incidents
documentation of the patient's receipt of his/her Bill of Rights
discharge planning/discharge summary
notification to authorized practitioner of changes in patient condition
The policy states that: the record is to be kept for 6 years after discharge
the record is to be kept for 6 years if a minor or 3 years after they reach age 18
if the agency discontinues operation, records are to be maintained, stored and access available
DOH will be informed of where the records are kept if the agency discontinues operation
Governing Authority (GA) policy/procedure – states that the GA: is responsible for management and operation of the agency
will ensure compliance with all applicable Federal, State and local statutes, rules and regulations
is responsible for adopting a budget
will adopt and approve amendments to written policies regarding management and operation of the agency and all services provided
will ensure the development of a written emergency plan
will ensure prompt submission of all records and reports required by the DOH
will make available to the public: information concerning services offered (agency brochure); geographic area servicing; fees for services; accepted insurances/payments
will maintain office facilities of sufficient size to conduct efficient business
will employ or contract for sufficient staff to conduct business and ensure quality of care provided
will employ a registered nurse to be responsible for direction/supervision of all patient care services and health care activities of the agency
will only accept patients whom the agency can provide safe and adequate services
will ensure the development and implementation of a patient complaint or grievance procedure
will maintain a record of complaints/concerns/grievances
will document receipt, investigation and the resolution of complaints
will provide a written response to all written complaints and to oral complaints, if requested, within 15 days of investigation findings
advise the complainant of the right to appeal
will review the appeal and notify the complainant within 30 days of the appeal
will be advised of the right to complain to the DOH
will establish a quality assessment and improvement program that involves all staff and the plan includes all aspects of care delivered
will appoint a Quality Improvement (QI) Committee that includes a consumer
will ensure continuous QI activities for all programs and services the agency provides
will assure the QI committee will meet at least 4 times a year
QI committee's activities are to: establish and oversee standards of care
review policies pertaining to health care services
conduct clinical record review of current patients
conduct clinical record review of discharged patients
review all complaints/grievances
prepare and submit a written summary of findings to the GA
Palliative Care policy/procedure – references: access to information and counseling appropriate to patients with life limiting conditions and illnesses
access to palliative care consultation and services including pain management
patients who lack capacity to make decisions
Contracts policy/procedure – the GA or operator is responsible for ensuring that the written contract includes: the services to be provided
how the services will be supervised and evaluated
charges and other financial arrangements
has a 'notwithstanding clause'
provisions for indemnification between the agency and the contract providers
that contract staff meet all personnel requirements
Health Commerce System (HCS) policy/procedure – states that: the agency is to obtain an HCS account for each agency operated
a sufficient number of knowledgeable staff will be available to maintain and keep current the account
the system will be accessed daily
the agency will have consistent coverage within the agency's hours of operation
the agency will have sufficient staff to ensure rapid response to requests for information from the State or local DOH
information will be current for the 24/7 Facility Contact and Office of the Administrator
the agency's communication directory will be kept current and updated

the agency will assign the following roles: Administrator; Director, Home Care Patient Services; Emergency Response Coordinator; HCS Coordinator; Criminal History Record Check Authorized Person (if providing aide services); Home Care Registry Agency Updater (if providing aide services); Home Care Registry Agency Viewer (if providing aide services)
Emergency Preparedness Plan policy/procedure – the plan addresses: types of emergencies that could impact patient care

maintaining a patient roster capturing: patient name, address and telephone number; emergency contact telephone number of family, caregiver and/or Healthcare Proxy; patient classification levels; Transportation Assistance Levels (TALs); identification of patients dependent on ventilator or electricity for health care needs
a 'Call Down' list of current staff and how that list will be kept current
a procedure for communications if telephone/computer network become unavailable
a contact list of community partners including: local health department; local emergency management; emergency medical services; local law enforcement
a procedure for how the agency will respond to requests for information by community partners
a procedure for participation in agency specific or community wide disaster drills and exercises
a procedure staff should employ when a patient refuses mandatory evacuation
Emergency Preparedness policies address: communications with the DOH through the HCS
responding to home care emergency response surveys
in-service of staff to the emergency preparedness plan at orientation and yearly (also with any revisions to the plan)
emergency response drills
a procedure to ensure patient contact information is current
alternate communications if telephones/internet unavailable
patient classification levels
Transportation Assistance Levels
Personnel policy/procedure – references: qualifications for all staff
verification of credentials
background checks of paraprofessional staff
employment verification/references (2)
personal identification
a signed and dated application
job descriptions for each position
performance evaluations and frequency
Personnel Health Requirements policy/procedure – references: pre-employment and annual health assessments
that the health status of all new personnel is assessed and documented prior to assuming patient care duties

the requirement that a statement asserting that the prospective employee is "free from impairment which is of potential risk to the patient or might interfere with the performance of his/her duties, including habituation or addiction to depressants, stimulants, narcotics, alcohol or drugs or substance which may alter the individual's behavior"

documentation of the following tests, examinations and immunizations pertaining to: rubella; measles (born on or after January 1, 1957); influenza; tuberculin skin test or blood assay level; annual health assessment
Orientation and Training policy/procedure – references training on: agency policy and procedures
HIV and blood-borne pathogens exposure plan
Infection Control, Universal Precautions, and use of protective equipment
HIV confidentiality and disclosure
yearly mandatory in-servicing
HIPPA [sic]
personal care aides must participate in 6 hours of in-service per year (home health aides, if approved: 12 hours)
Influenza Vaccination policy/procedure – references: the influenza season as determined by the Commissioner
the documentation of vaccination status of all personnel
procedures for unvaccinated personnel with direct patient contact including supervision
education and wearing of a surgical/procedure mask for all unvaccinated personnel with direct patient contact
HIV / Blood Borne Pathogens policy/procedure – references: implementation and enforcement for the prevention of HIV or other blood borne pathogens transmission
Universal Precautions
yearly mandatory in-servicing
post-exposure testing
post-exposure counseling
confidentiality
personal protective equipment
a designated person to be reported to for exposure
appropriate medical follow-up for an exposed individual
system for monitoring prevention programs
investigation of exposure
Criminal History Record Check (CHRC) policy/procedure – references: the designation of CHRC authorized persons
confidentiality
who is subject to a CHRC
employee rights including informed consent
process for requesting and obtaining fingerprints including timeframes
supervision of temporary personnel awaiting determinations
documentation of supervision
procedures for Hold in Abeyance, Pending or Final Determination letters
process for reporting terminations and separations to the Department
retention, confidentiality, and separation of personnel records
Home Care Registry (HCR) policy/procedure – includes that: the HCR must be accessed for any worker who began their training on or after September 25, 2009
a worker may not begin to provide services until the HCR been [sic] accessed
a worker may not begin to provide services until their information has been posted to the HCR
the worker's information must be posted with [sic] 10 business days of starting employment with the agency
the agency must update the registry within 10 business days with any corrections requested by the worker
the agency must update the registry within 10 business days of the worker's termination
Records and/or Reports policy/procedure – references: record/report retention including retention time frames; where the records will be retained; what records and reports will be retained

records/reports to be retained: license issued by the Department; certificate of incorporation (if applicable); partnership agreement (if applicable); certificate of doing business under an assumed name (if applicable); contracts/agreements related to patient care; rules and bylaws of the governing authority; operating policies and procedures; current patient roster; listing of all personnel

Records to be maintained and made available to DOH upon request: governing authority meeting minutes; committee meeting minutes; records of all financial transactions related to patient care; personnel records; patient clinical records; grievances/complaints; all records related to patient care/services which must be retained for 3 years, will be maintained in hard copy or electronic form, and will be secured

The agency will make available to the Department annually: statistical summaries; list of stockholders and shareholders of the corporation (if applicable); list of directors, officers and/or corporate members (if applicable); documents related to Securities and Exchange Commission (if applicable)
Infection Control policy/procedure – references: Universal Precautions/Standard Precautions
a procedure preventing the spread of infection
handwashing
nursing bag management and technique
home health aide bag technique
reporting of communicable disease
occupational exposure control
Change of Ownership policy/procedure – references: what constitutes a change of ownership/transfer of interests/stock/acquisition
notification to the Department
submission of application to the Department
approval by the Public Health and Health Planning Council
Amendment of the License policy/procedure – references: what constitutes an amendment (for example: adding a service or change in location)
notification to and approval by the Department
submitting required materials to the Department as applicable

Policy and Procedure Manual with Index/Table of Contents: listing of all agency policies, including Policy Name, Policy Number and Initial/Revision Date; Index/TOC cross references corresponding regulations; manual paginated correctly; correct agency name used throughout the manual

A job description and a policy and procedure (P & P) for each service requested and approved by PHHPC. Listed: Nursing (marked 'X' as approved by PHHPC), Home Health Aide, Personal Care Aide, Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy, Respiratory Therapy, Speech/Language Pathology, Audiology, Medical Social Work, Physician Services, Nutrition, Homemaker, Housekeeper, Medical Supply Equipment/Appliances
At a minimum a policy/procedure for: Patient Rights; Complaint Procedure; Admission; Discharge/Discharge Planning; Plan of Care; Assessment; Medical Orders; Clinical Supervision; Clinical Records

At a minimum a policy/procedure for (continued): Quality Assurance and Quality Improvement Program; Contract Procedure; Health Commerce System; Personnel; Criminal History Record Check (if providing aide services); Home Care Registry (if providing aide services); Infection Control/Blood borne Pathogen; Change of Ownership/Amendment of License; Governing Authority; Emergency Preparedness; Others as applicable

Program materials the agency must have submitted: Emergency Preparedness Plan; Admission packet/Start of Care packet; Agency brochure; Patient 'Bill of Rights'; Clinical record forms (Assessment/Reassessment, Plan of Care, Physician Orders, Aide Activity Sheet (if applicable), 'Aide Care Plan' (if applicable)); Personnel record forms. (Part A also lists the Federal Tax ID number, QI Committee member names and titles, and ALP forms; those are administrative and not policy content.)

Required elements of EACH policy: Agency Name (as on the PHHPC-approved application); Policy number (discretely numbered); Title; Policy Statement/Purpose; Date (policy date and revision date); Page Number (e.g., 1 of 4 pages); Authority (statute, regulation and policy); Application (who or what the policy applies to); Responsible Party (title, position or department including contact information); Terminology (terms unique to the policy defined); Cross reference to other agency policies

Procedure (each policy includes a step-by-step procedure): 1. An overview of the procedure, if appropriate. 2. Identification of any necessary skills and/or materials needed. 3. A logical sequence of steps and sub-steps in the order they should occur. 4. Use of diagrams, illustrations or examples, if appropriate.
